claims.text: In Portugal, INFARMED may authorise exceptional use (AUE) of a medicine without a marketing authorisation, for example when it is clinically justified as indispensable and no authorised alternative exists (Estatuto do Medicamento, Art 92).
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "O INFARMED, I.P., pode autorizar a utilização em Portugal de medicamento não possuidor de qualquer das restantes autorizações previstas no presente decreto-lei … a) Mediante justificação clínica, sejam considerados imprescindíveis à prevenção, diagnóstico ou tratamento de determinadas patologias, desde que seja demonstrada a inexistência de alternativa no conjunto de medicamentos com autorização de introdução no mercado;" (English: "INFARMED may authorise the use in Portugal of a medicine holding none of the other authorisations provided for in this decree-law … a) where, on clinical justification, they are considered indispensable for preventing, diagnosing or treating certain conditions, provided it is shown that no alternative exists among medicines with a marketing authorisation;") · grader: research agents under the jurisdiction research brief; statements are regulatory facts, graded context

claims.text: In Portugal, a patient-specific AUE is granted to institutions authorised to buy medicines directly (e.g., hospitals) or used by community pharmacies under set conditions, and always requires an individual clinical justification that the medicine is indispensable (INFARMED Deliberação 840/2023, 31 Aug 2023).
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "A AUE destinada a doente específico pode ser concedida às entidades com autorização de aquisição direta de medicamentos … 3 — As autorizações previstas no presente artigo carecem de comprovação da imprescindibilidade do medicamento face às alternativas terapêuticas, mediante justificação clínica individualizada." (English: "A patient-specific AUE may be granted to entities authorised for direct purchase of medicines … 3 — The authorisations provided for in this article require proof that the medicine is indispensable compared with therapeutic alternatives, by means of an individualised clinical justification.") · grader: research agents under the jurisdiction research brief; statements are regulatory facts, graded context

claims.text: In Portugal, INFARMED told prescribers in July 2024 that Ozempic, Trulicity and Victoza should not be prescribed to people without diabetes, because off-label use (notably for weight loss) threatens supply for diabetic patients (Circular 045/CD/100.20.200, 4 Jul 2024).
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "Os medicamentos Ozempic, Trulicity e Victoza não devem ser prescritos a doentes que não sejam diabéticos;" (English: "Ozempic, Trulicity and Victoza must not be prescribed to patients who are not diabetic;") · grader: research agents under the jurisdiction research brief; statements are regulatory facts, graded context

claims.text: In Portugal, a medicine is any substance presented as treating or preventing disease or used to restore, correct or modify physiological functions by pharmacological, immunological or metabolic action, so a 'research use only' label does not take such a product outside medicines law (Estatuto do Medicamento, Art 3).
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "«Medicamento», toda a substância ou associação de substâncias apresentada como possuindo propriedades curativas ou preventivas de doenças em seres humanos ou dos seus sintomas ou que possa ser utilizada ou administrada no ser humano com vista a estabelecer um diagnóstico médico ou, exercendo uma ação farmacológica, imunológica ou metabólica, a restaurar, corrigir ou modificar funções fisiológicas;" (English: "'Medicine': any substance or combination of substances presented as having properties for treating or preventing disease in human beings or its symptoms, or which may be used in or administered to human beings with a view to making a medical diagnosis or to restoring, correcting or modifying physiological functions by exerting a pharmacological, immunological or metabolic action;") · grader: research agents under the jurisdiction research brief; statements are regulatory facts, graded context

claims.text: In Portugal, placing any medicine on the market requires authorisation by INFARMED's governing body, unless the law provides otherwise (e.g., EU central authorisation) (Estatuto do Medicamento, Art 14(1)).
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "Salvo disposição em contrário, a comercialização de medicamentos no território nacional está sujeita a autorização do órgão máximo do INFARMED." (English: "Unless otherwise provided, the marketing of medicines in national territory is subject to authorisation by INFARMED's governing body.") · grader: research agents under the jurisdiction research brief; statements are regulatory facts, graded context

claims.text: In Portugal, making, selling, supplying or administering medicines without the required authorisation, or falsified medicines, is an administrative offence fined from €2,000 up to 15% of turnover or €180,000, whichever is lower (Estatuto do Medicamento, Art 181(2)(a)).
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "Constitui contraordenação, punível com coima entre (euro) 2 000 e 15 % do volume de negócios do responsável ou (euro) 180 000, consoante o que for inferior: a) O fabrico, introdução no mercado, comercialização, distribuição, intermediação, importação, exportação, importação paralela, dispensa, fornecimento ou venda ao público, ou administração de medicamentos ou medicamentos experimentais, bem como de substâncias ativas ou excipientes, sem as autorizações, ou registos, exigidas ou que sejam medicamentos falsificados;" (English: "It is an administrative offence, punishable by a fine between €2,000 and 15% of the offender's turnover or €180,000, whichever is lower: a) the manufacture, placing on the market, marketing, distribution, brokering, import, export, parallel import, dispensing, supply or sale to the public, or administration of medicines or investigational medicines, or of active substances or excipients, without the required authorisations or registrations, or that are falsified medicines;") · grader: research agents under the jurisdiction research brief; statements are regulatory facts, graded context

claims.text: In Portugal, INFARMED does not authorise the import of medicines for personal use (Circular 148/CD, 29 Jul 2011).
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "Assim, o Infarmed não autoriza a importação de medicamentos para uso pessoal." (English: "Therefore, Infarmed does not authorise the import of medicines for personal use.") · grader: research agents under the jurisdiction research brief; statements are regulatory facts, graded context

claims.text: In Portugal, INFARMED is the national competent authority for cosmetic products under the EU Cosmetics Regulation (Decreto-Lei 23/2025 of 19 March 2025).
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "O INFARMED — Autoridade Nacional do Medicamento e Produtos de Saúde, I. P. (INFARMED, I. P.), é a autoridade nacional competente para efeitos do n.º 1 do artigo 34.º do Regulamento (CE) n.º 1223/2009 e do presente decreto-lei." (English: "INFARMED — National Authority of Medicines and Health Products, I.P., is the national competent authority for the purposes of Article 34(1) of Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 and of this decree-law.") · grader: research agents under the jurisdiction research brief; statements are regulatory facts, graded context

claims.text: In Portugal, INFARMED states that products administered by ingestion, inhalation, injection or implantation are not cosmetics, so an injected 'peptide' cannot be sold as a cosmetic (INFARMED cosmetics FAQ, read 25 Sep 2026).
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "Não são considerados cosméticos produtos cuja administração se faça por ingestão, inalação, injeção ou implantação no corpo." (English: "Products administered by ingestion, inhalation, injection or implantation into the body are not considered cosmetics.") · grader: research agents under the jurisdiction research brief; statements are regulatory facts, graded context

claims.text: In Portugal, borderline products (such as topical 'peptide' serums with medicinal-sounding claims) must be classified case by case by the Responsible Person, using the European Commission borderline manual; cosmetics need no prior authorisation but are subject to INFARMED market surveillance (INFARMED cosmetics FAQ).
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "Os produtos fronteira devem ser avaliados caso a caso pela Pessoa Responsável, tendo em conta todas as suas características." (English: "Borderline products must be assessed case by case by the Responsible Person, taking all their characteristics into account.") · grader: research agents under the jurisdiction research brief; statements are regulatory facts, graded context

claims.text: In Portugal, food supplements are intended to maintain the body's homeostasis, not to prevent, treat or cure disease (DGAV, read 25 Sep 2026).
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "Os suplementos alimentares destinam-se a manter a homeostasia do organismo e não à prevenção, tratamento ou cura de doenças." (English: "Food supplements are intended to maintain the body's homeostasis and not to prevent, treat or cure diseases.") · grader: research agents under the jurisdiction research brief; statements are regulatory facts, graded context

claims.text: In Portugal, every food supplement must be notified to DGAV before it is placed on the national market, even if already sold in another EU Member State (DGAV, read 25 Sep 2026).
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "Os Suplementos Alimentares têm de ser notificados à DGAV , antes de serem colocados no mercado nacional, mesmo os que já se encontram comercializados noutro Estado-Membro da UE" (English: "Food supplements must be notified to DGAV before being placed on the national market, even those already marketed in another EU Member State") · grader: research agents under the jurisdiction research brief; statements are regulatory facts, graded context

claims.text: In Portugal, DGAV warns that notifying a supplement does not mean it is authorised or compliant; there is no pre-market evaluation and control is by later sampling (DGAV, read 25 Sep 2026).
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "em caso algum, o operador poderá concluir que o produto se encontra autorizado ou que se encontra conforme." (English: "in no case may the operator conclude that the product is authorised or compliant.") · grader: research agents under the jurisdiction research brief; statements are regulatory facts, graded context

claims.text: In Portugal, advertising any medicine that lacks a valid authorisation for the national market, or that is used only under an exceptional-use authorisation (Arts 92-93), is prohibited (Estatuto do Medicamento, Art 152(1)).
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "É proibida a publicidade de medicamentos que não sejam objecto de uma autorização ou registo válidos para o mercado nacional ou que tenham sido autorizados ao abrigo do artigo 92.º e 93.º" (English: "Advertising of medicines that do not hold a valid authorisation or registration for the national market, or that were authorised under Articles 92 and 93, is prohibited") · grader: research agents under the jurisdiction research brief; statements are regulatory facts, graded context

claims.text: In Portugal, advertising prescription-only medicines to the general public is prohibited; they may be advertised only in technical publications or media intended for and accessible only to health professionals (Estatuto do Medicamento, Arts 152(2) and 154(1)).
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "É proibida a publicidade junto do público em geral dos medicamentos: a) Sujeitos a receita médica; … Os medicamentos sujeitos a receita médica só podem ser anunciados ou publicitados em publicações técnicas ou suportes de informação destinados e acessíveis exclusivamente por médicos e outros profissionais de saúde." (English: "Advertising to the general public of the following medicines is prohibited: a) those subject to medical prescription; … Prescription-only medicines may only be announced or advertised in technical publications or information media intended for and accessible exclusively to physicians and other health professionals.") · grader: research agents under the jurisdiction research brief; statements are regulatory facts, graded context

claims.text: In Portugal, the advertiser, the advertising agency, anyone disseminating the advertising and the owner of the advertising medium are all liable for breaches of the medicine-advertising rules, which can also bring publication of the sanction and a suspension of the medicine's advertising for up to two years (Estatuto do Medicamento, Art 182).
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "São punidos como autores ou coautores das contraordenações previstas no presente decreto-lei, relativamente à violação dos deveres previstos no capítulo IX, o anunciante, a agência de publicidade ou qualquer outra entidade que exerça a atividade publicitária, ou a divulgação de publicidade, o titular do suporte publicitário ou o respetivo concessionário." (English: "The advertiser, the advertising agency or any other entity carrying out the advertising activity or disseminating the advertising, and the owner of the advertising medium or its concessionaire, are punished as perpetrators or co-perpetrators of the offences under this decree-law concerning breaches of the duties in Chapter IX.") · grader: research agents under the jurisdiction research brief; statements are regulatory facts, graded context

claims.text: In Portugal, advertising of health services by any provider, public or private (including clinics offering aesthetic treatments), is regulated by Decreto-Lei 238/2015, which bans false claims of guaranteed cure or results or of absence of side effects.
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "São proibidas as práticas de publicidade em saúde que, por qualquer razão, induzam ou sejam suscetíveis de induzir em erro o utente quanto à decisão a adotar, designadamente: … c) Se refiram falsamente a demonstrações ou garantias de cura ou de resultados ou sem efeitos adversos ou secundários;" (English: "Health advertising practices that, for any reason, mislead or are liable to mislead the user as to the decision to take are prohibited, namely those that: … c) falsely refer to demonstrations or guarantees of cure or of results, or of absence of adverse or side effects;") · grader: research agents under the jurisdiction research brief; statements are regulatory facts, graded context

claims.text: In Portugal, the health regulator ERS (Entidade Reguladora da Saúde) enforces the health-advertising rules, with fines of €250–€3,740.98 for individuals and €1,000–€44,891.81 for companies, plus possible bans of up to two years (Decreto-Lei 238/2015, Art 8).
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "Cabe à Entidade Reguladora da Saúde a fiscalização e a instrução dos processos de contraordenação, competindo ao respetivo conselho de administração a aplicação das correspondentes coimas e sanções acessórias." (English: "The Health Regulatory Authority is responsible for supervision and for investigating the offence proceedings, and its board of directors applies the corresponding fines and ancillary sanctions.") · grader: research agents under the jurisdiction research brief; statements are regulatory facts, graded context

claims.text: In Portugal, every medicine intended for parenteral administration (injection) is prescription-only by law (Estatuto do Medicamento, Art 114(1)(d)).
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "Estão sujeitos a receita médica os medicamentos que preencham uma das seguintes condições: … d) Destinem-se a ser administrados por via parentérica." (English: "Medicines meeting one of the following conditions are subject to medical prescription: … d) they are intended for parenteral administration.") · grader: research agents under the jurisdiction research brief; statements are regulatory facts, graded context

claims.text: In Portugal, 'restricted prescription' medicines (MSRM restrita) are reserved to specialised settings: alínea a) means exclusive hospital use (e.g., Olumiant, Scenesse) and alínea b) means conditions diagnosed only in hospital or specialised settings (e.g., somatropin) (Estatuto do Medicamento, Art 118).
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "a) Destinarem-se a uso exclusivo hospitalar, devido às suas características farmacológicas, à sua novidade, ou por razões de saúde pública; b) Destinarem-se a patologias cujo diagnóstico seja efectuado apenas em meio hospitalar ou estabelecimentos diferenciados com meios de diagnóstico adequados," (English: "a) they are intended for exclusive hospital use because of their pharmacological characteristics, their novelty, or for public-health reasons; b) they are intended for conditions whose diagnosis is made only in hospital or in specialised establishments with appropriate diagnostic means,") · grader: research agents under the jurisdiction research brief; statements are regulatory facts, graded context

claims.text: In Portugal, growth hormone is distributed free of charge through hospitals with endocrinology or paediatric services, and a national commission (CNNHC) sets the conditions for its administration (INFARMED, read 25 Sep 2026).
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "À Comissão Nacional para a Normalização da Hormona do Crescimento compete a definição das condições de administração da hormona de crescimento, que é distribuída gratuitamente nas instituições hospitalares com serviços de endocrinologia e/ou serviços de pediatria," (English: "The National Commission for the Standardisation of Growth Hormone is responsible for defining the conditions of administration of growth hormone, which is distributed free of charge in hospital institutions with endocrinology and/or paediatric services,") · grader: research agents under the jurisdiction research brief; statements are regulatory facts, graded context

claims.text: In Portugal, INFARMED relayed on 5 Sep 2025 the EMA/HMA warning of a sharp rise in illegal online sales of products presented as GLP-1 agonists (semaglutide, liraglutide, tirzepatide), promoted on social media and not authorised.
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "Nos últimos meses, verificou-se um aumento acentuado na comercialização ilegal de medicamentos apresentados como agonistas do recetor GLP-1 – como o semaglutido, o liraglutido e a tirzepatida – destinados à perda de peso e ao tratamento da diabetes." (English: "In recent months there has been a sharp increase in the illegal marketing of medicines presented as GLP-1 receptor agonists – such as semaglutide, liraglutide and tirzepatide – intended for weight loss and the treatment of diabetes.") · grader: research agents under the jurisdiction research brief; statements are regulatory facts, graded context

claims.text: In Portugal, INFARMED stated in Sep 2025 that medicines can be bought online only on the websites of pharmacies and licensed non-prescription outlets, and that GLP-1 agonists are prescription-only medicines sold only in pharmacies.
claims.reviewNote: primary source quote: "Em Portugal, a aquisição de medicamentos na internet só é possível nos sites das farmácias e LVMNSRM." (English: "In Portugal, medicines can only be bought on the internet from the websites of pharmacies and LVMNSRM (licensed non-prescription medicine outlets).") · grader: research agents under the jurisdiction research brief; statements are regulatory facts, graded context

claims.text: The skin works as a peripheral neuro-immuno-endocrine organ: reviews describe four immuno-endocrine units (epidermal, dermal, hypodermal, adnexal) whose cells make and respond to hormones and signal to neighbouring cells, through sensory nerves, and through the circulation. This is a mechanistic framework drawn from cell, tissue and animal work.

claims.text: Skin cells carry the enzymes to make steroids from cholesterol (CYP11A1) and to activate circulating precursors (11β-HSD1, 5α-reductase, aromatase), producing cortisol, DHT and estradiol locally; this rests mainly on cell, tissue and biochemical studies.
claims.reviewNote: the guide itself calls this literature 'mechanistic … not a dosing rationale' · grader: Graded 2026-09-24 by the agent under Omar Saleem's delegation ("you should be able to do that from the guide"); rule set below; final review Dr. Hannah-Shmouni

The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide treats the aesthetic exam as a systemic screen and lists suspected Cushing syndrome (violaceous striae, central obesity, proximal weakness, new hypertension or diabetes) and rapidly progressive virilisation among reasons to refer promptly to endocrinology.

claims.text: The Hormone Cell Atlas (Science 2026) analysed RNA for 379 hormone and receptor genes in about 14 million single cells and nuclei from 47 human tissues, skin among them, and mapped putative hormone-producing and hormone-receiving cell types.

claims.text: In 178 adults of the Leiden Longevity Study, more p16-positive cells in sun-protected arm skin were associated with ageing-type elastic fibres, more facial wrinkles and higher perceived age independent of chronological age; people in the lowest tertile of epidermal p16 counts looked about 3 years younger than those in the highest. This is an association, not evidence of cause.

claims.text: Skin collagen falls with age; aged human dermis shows more fibroblast MMP-1, fragmented collagen and fibroblasts under less mechanical tension that make less procollagen, and culture work shows fragmentation feeds back to raise MMP-1. That senescent cells drive this in living skin is plausible but not shown.

claims.text: Causal evidence that senescent cells drive ageing comes from mice: clearing p16-positive cells extended healthy lifespan and senolytics improved function and survival in old mice; skin was checked only for safety (thickness, fibrosis, wound closure), and clearing p16-positive cells during healing slowed wound closure.

claims.text: Human senotherapy data are small pilots with tissue-marker endpoints — an open-label senolytic pilot in 9 patients reduced epidermal p16/p21-positive cells; an exploratory topical rapamycin RCT (36 enrolled, 19 lost) reduced skin p16 — clinical improvement in that trial was described only in 'multiple participants', and no adequately sized trial with clinical skin-ageing outcomes was found on PubMed or ClinicalTrials.gov (checked 24 September 2026). The guide advises that senolytics generally be confined to clinical trials.

title.en: The skin as an endocrine organ, and how it ages

summary.en: The skin as an endocrine organ; four immuno-endocrine microenvironments; local peripheral endocrine axes (HPA, thyroid, somatotropic, melanocortin); Hormone Cell Atlas cutaneous receptor distribution; endocrine senescence and SASP pathophysiology.

objective.en: By the end, you can analyze the autonomous neuro-immuno-endocrine physiology of the skin and evaluate how local steroidogenesis, receptor expression, and cellular senescence drive structural dermal aging.

title.en: The skin as an endocrine organ, and how it ages

description.en: Lesson 1.1 The skin as a steroidogenic, endocrine organ · Lesson 1.2 Receptor maps and what they prove · Lesson 1.3 Senescence, the SASP and the ageing dermis.

units.tutorContext: Module 1 teaches cutaneous neuro-immuno-endocrine physiology with every finding labelled by evidence type (mechanism, human evidence, regulatory status, open question). The skin is described as four immuno-endocrine units (epidermal, dermal, hypodermal, adnexal) that signal locally, via sensory nerves and via the circulation (mechanism reviews, D). Skin cells express CYP11A1, 11β-HSD1, 5α-reductase and aromatase and make cortisol, DHT and estradiol locally (cell/tissue work, D); human scalp follicles run an HPA-like loop with cortisol secretion and CRH feedback ex vivo (Ito 2005) and a GH/IGF-1 loop ex vivo (Horesh 2023); keratinocyte glucocorticoids restrain skin inflammation in mice (Phan 2021); the thyroid-like loop is mostly mouse data. Three directions: local loop; body to skin (Cushing striae, hypothyroid skin); skin to body (vitamin D3 released into the circulation, established human physiology; a skin contribution to circulating sex steroids per reviews). Refer systemic patterns promptly (violaceous striae with new hypertension or diabetes, rapid virilisation), per the Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide. The Hormone Cell Atlas (Fei, Huang-Doran et al., Science 2026) read RNA of 379 hormone/receptor genes in ~14 million cells and nuclei from 47 tissues incl. skin; its authors call the predictions putative and hypothesis-generating: RNA is not protein, secretion or clinical effect. The guide's pearl that serum 25(OH)D falls with sunscreen use is not borne out by field trials of daily moderate-SPF sunscreen (Neale 2019, C; high SPF untested); never advise dropping sun protection. Senescence: p16-positive cells rise with age in human epidermis and dermis (C) and track with wrinkles and perceived age (Waaijer 2016, n=178, association, C); the SASP was defined in cultured cells (D); an MMP-1 collagen-fragmentation loop is shown in aged human dermis plus culture (D), with senescent cells a plausible, unproven driver; clearing senescent cells extends healthy lifespan in mice (D); human senotherapy data are small biomarker pilots (Hickson 2019 open-label n=9, D; Chung 2019 topical rapamycin exploratory RCT, C); no randomized trial with clinical skin-ageing outcomes (checked Sept 2026); the guide confines senolytics to trials. Levers with human trials: daily sunscreen (Hughes 2013, n=903, B), topical tretinoin for photoageing (GRADE A), retinol in very old skin (Kafi 2007, C). Never give doses, concentrations, regimens or sourcing; adapt 'what you do next' to the learner's role (prescriber, clinical staff, advisor) without changing evidence. No CME credit is currently offered.

learningObjectives.en: Characterize local steroidogenesis and the autonomous peripheral neuroendocrine axes operating within epidermal, dermal, hypodermal, and adnexal compartments.
Differentiate between transcriptomic hormone receptor predictions and validated endocrine secretion across cutaneous cell lineages.
Assess how senescent cutaneous cell accumulation and the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) impair extracellular matrix maintenance and accelerate dermal thinning.

lead.en: Hormones and Peptides for Skin · Module 01

title.en: The skin makes its own hormones.

body.en: This course starts with physiology, because every later question about a hormone or peptide for skin rests on it. Skin senses hormones from the blood, makes several of its own, and ages in ways that change both. In three lessons you will separate what happens locally in the skin from what the rest of the body sends in, and label each finding by the kind of evidence behind it.

points.en: 1.1 The skin as a steroidogenic, endocrine organ
1.2 Receptor maps: what a cell atlas can and cannot show
1.3 Senescence, the SASP and the ageing dermis

title.en: The skin as an endocrine organ, and how it ages

blocks.sourceNote: Slominski 2025 · Slominski & Wortsman 2000 · Zouboulis 2004 · Roosterman 2006 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 5–6

videoTranscript.en: This course starts with physiology, because every later question about a hormone or peptide for skin rests on it. Skin senses hormones from the blood, makes several of its own, and ages in ways that change both. Think of the skin as a sensing organ with its own hormone supply. Researchers who study it describe four units, epidermal, dermal, hypodermal and adnexal, the last meaning hair follicles and glands. Each unit holds cells that can make hormones and mount an immune response, such as keratinocytes, fibroblasts, sebocytes, fat cells and mast cells. Signals move three ways. Neighbouring cells talk directly, sensory nerves carry messages in and out, and some products enter the blood and reach distant organs. Keep one distinction in view for the whole module. A signal that is made and used inside the skin is a local loop. A hormone that arrives from the blood, or leaves the skin for the rest of the body, is systemic signalling.

title.en: How will you use this course?

body.en: The evidence and grades are the same for everyone, and regulatory notes follow the country you choose. What changes with your role, in every module, is the 'what you do next' at the end of each lesson, so it fits what your licence lets you do.

body.en: Recent reviews describe the skin as a neuro-immuno-endocrine organ built from four units: epidermal, dermal, hypodermal and adnexal (hair follicles and glands). Each holds cells that can make hormones and mount an immune response. They signal to neighbouring cells, through sensory nerves, and through the blood. Most of this picture comes from cell, tissue and animal studies.

Three routes: neighbour to neighbour, nerve, bloodstream

body.en: Epidermis, dermis, subcutis and the adnexa each hold cells that make hormones and cells that react to them, from keratinocytes and fibroblasts to fat cells and mast cells.
Signals pass between neighbouring cells, along sensory nerves, and into the blood, where they can reach distant organs.
The framework is drawn from cell, tissue and animal work. It explains how skin behaves; each finding in this module is labelled by the evidence behind it.

Researchers who study it describe four units, epidermal, dermal, hypodermal and adnexal, the last meaning hair follicles and glands. Each unit holds cells that can make hormones and mount an immune response, such as keratinocytes, fibroblasts, sebocytes, fat cells and mast cells. Signals move three ways. Neighbouring cells talk directly, sensory nerves carry messages in and out, and some products enter the blood and reach distant organs. Keep one distinction in view for the whole module. A signal that is made and used inside the skin is a local loop. A hormone that arrives from the blood, or leaves the skin for the rest of the body, is systemic signalling. Much of what follows is mechanism, drawn from cell, tissue and animal studies, and each finding will be labelled that way.

title.en: Read the skin before the serum.

body.en: The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide treats the aesthetic exam as a systemic screen. Sudden thinning and easy bruising suggest cortisol excess; coarse, dry, cool skin suggests hypothyroidism; new acanthosis nigricans flags insulin resistance. It lists violaceous striae with new hypertension or diabetes, and rapidly progressive virilisation, among reasons to refer promptly to endocrinology. Local skin biology explains how skin behaves; it does not justify prescribing a hormone.

points.en: A skin sign can be the first sign of a systemic disorder
Some patterns need prompt endocrine referral
Local loops explain biology; they do not justify treatment

blocks.sourceNote: Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 5 clinical pearl and referral list · Safer 2011

body.en: Thinning and bruising, coarse dry skin, new acanthosis nigricans: each points to a systemic axis before it points to a serum.
The guide lists violaceous striae with new hypertension or diabetes, rapid virilisation and signs of an endocrine tumour as reasons to refer promptly.
Local loops explain how skin behaves day to day. The guide calls them foundation, never a reason to dose anyone with a hormone.

audioScript.en: Picture the consultation where a patient asks about thinning, bruising skin. The Aesthetic and Regenerative Endocrinology guide asks you to read that skin as a window on the whole endocrine system before reaching for a serum. Sudden thinning with easy bruising suggests cortisol excess. Coarse, dry, cool skin suggests an underactive thyroid. New acanthosis nigricans points to insulin resistance. The guide lists violaceous striae with new hypertension or diabetes, rapidly progressive virilisation, and signs of an endocrine tumour as reasons to refer promptly to endocrinology. The local loops from the last two moments explain how skin behaves day to day. They are foundation biology, and the guide is explicit that they are no rationale for dosing anyone with a hormone. Whatever your role, a systemic pattern in the skin gets a systemic answer.

prescriber.en: When a skin pattern suggests a systemic disorder, assess or refer before any cosmetic plan, and record that you considered it. Local skin biology is no basis for prescribing a hormone for appearance.

clinical-staff.en: If you see new striae, rapid bruising, sudden hair change or signs of virilisation, record them and raise them with the prescriber before the next treatment.

advisor.en: If a client's skin change comes with new systemic symptoms, suggest they see a prescriber before trying another product. A serum cannot answer a systemic question.

prompt.en: Fictional case. A 52-year-old has new thin, easily bruised skin on her forearms, new violaceous striae and newly raised blood pressure. She has read that skin makes its own cortisol and asks whether a cream could calm it. Which reading is right?

text.en: Her skin's own cortisol explains the picture, so the answer is local.

why.en: Local skin cortisol tunes immune activity where it is made. It does not explain new striae together with new hypertension.

text.en: The combination is a systemic pattern; the guide lists it as a reason for prompt endocrine referral before any skin treatment.

why.en: Correct. Striae, bruising and new hypertension together point to possible systemic cortisol excess: a body-to-skin signal.

text.en: Local and systemic cortisol are interchangeable, so either explanation fits.

why.en: Local synthesis acts within the skin and runs its own feedback; a systemic syndrome needs a systemic assessment.

feedback.en: Decide which direction the signal runs before you decide what to treat.

title.en: A map of fourteen million cells.

body.en: The Hormone Cell Atlas, published in Science in 2026, read the RNA for 379 hormone and receptor genes in about 14 million single cells and nuclei from 47 human tissues, skin among them. From that RNA it predicted which cell types could make a hormone and which could respond to one. It is a map of predicted capacity; it did not measure hormone release.

points.en: RNA for 379 hormone and receptor genes
About 14 million cells and nuclei, 47 tissues
Output: predicted producers and receivers

blocks.sourceNote: Fei & Huang-Doran et al., Science 2026 · hormonecellatlas.org.uk · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 7

body.en: RNA for 379 hormone and receptor genes, cell by cell, across 47 human tissues including skin.
Which cell types could make a hormone and which could respond, including unexpected sites outside the classic glands.
Whether a cell actually makes and releases the hormone, and whether that hormone does anything there.

audioScript.en: Fourteen million cells is the scale of the Hormone Cell Atlas, a Cambridge-led study published in Science in 2026. The team read the RNA for 379 hormone and receptor genes in single cells and nuclei from forty-seven human tissues, skin included. From those readings they scored each cell type for its predicted capacity to make or to receive a hormone, and they flagged unexpected sites, such as RNA for the gut hormone secretin in a type of immune cell. The Aesthetic and Regenerative Endocrinology guide uses the atlas to argue that the skin, built from every major cell lineage, is plausibly one of the body's largest distributed signalling networks. The word plausibly matters. Everything in the atlas starts from RNA, and RNA tells you what a cell could make. Whether the cell actually makes and releases the hormone is the question the rest of this lesson answers.

doesNot.en: It does not show that a skin cell secretes a hormone, how much, or that the hormone acts there. A receptor gene on the map is not evidence that a product aimed at it works.

title.en: A map to confirm, then a trial.

body.en: Topical and transdermal treatments act through receptors the skin already carries, and the skin's own enzymes change how strongly a hormone acts, so the skin's response need not mirror the dose. A receptor on a map is where an efficacy question starts. The same caution applies to physiology you think you know: the guide says serum vitamin D falls with sunscreen use, yet field trials of daily sunscreen did not lower it.

points.en: A receptor on the map is a hypothesis
Local enzymes change potency in skin
Daily-sunscreen field trials did not lower vitamin D

blocks.sourceNote: Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 6–7 pearls · Neale 2019 · Fei 2026 · Bikle 2014

body.en: Receptors explain how a topical could act. Whether it does is a question for a human trial.
Steroid-metabolising enzymes in skin change potency, so the response in skin can differ from what the dose predicts.
Artificial-UV experiments show sunscreen blocks vitamin D synthesis; field trials of daily use did not lower blood levels. High-protection products have not been trialled.

audioScript.en: Two habits follow from the atlas. The first concerns product claims. Topical and transdermal treatments act through receptors the skin already carries, and the skin's own enzymes change how strongly a hormone acts once it arrives, so the response in skin can differ from what the dose predicts. A receptor on a map is where an efficacy question starts, and the answer still needs a trial. The second habit concerns the physiology you think you know. The guide's testing pearl says serum vitamin D falls with sunscreen use, which the biology predicts. An independent review found that in real-life field trials, daily sunscreen did not lower blood levels, although the sunscreens tested were moderate and today's high-protection products have never been trialled. Keep recommending sun protection, and treat vitamin D as its own question.

prescriber.en: When a product or protocol is justified by 'skin has receptors for it', ask for the human trial before you prescribe. Assess vitamin D on clinical grounds, and do not advise patients to drop sun protection.

clinical-staff.en: If a patient says they stopped sunscreen to raise their vitamin D, note it and pass it to the prescriber; the trials do not support stopping.

advisor.en: Describe receptor-based product claims as hypotheses unless a human trial backs them, keep sun-protection advice unchanged, and send vitamin D questions to a prescriber.

why.en: The finding concerns a receptor, and RNA says nothing about secretion or deficiency.

title.en: Cells that stop dividing and keep talking.

body.en: A senescent cell has stopped dividing for good but stays metabolically active, releasing cytokines, matrix-degrading enzymes and growth factors: the senescence-associated secretory phenotype, or SASP. The SASP was characterised in cultured cells. In human skin, cells carrying the senescence marker p16INK4a become more common with age in both epidermis and dermis.

points.en: Senescent: permanent arrest, still secreting
SASP (IL-6, IL-8, MMPs, growth factors): defined in culture
Human skin: p16-positive cells rise with age

blocks.sourceNote: Coppé 2008 · Ressler 2006 · Ho & Dreesen 2021 · Wang & Dreesen 2018 · Haykal 2026 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 7

body.en: A damaged cell stops dividing for good, which guards against cancer and helps wound repair.
It stays active and releases inflammatory cytokines, matrix-degrading enzymes and growth factors, first catalogued in cultured human cells.

title.en: What we see in human skin

body.en: Older skin holds more cells carrying the marker p16 in epidermis and dermis. No single marker is definitive.

audioScript.en: Senescence begins as a safety mechanism. A cell that has taken enough damage stops dividing for good, which helps guard against cancer and is useful during wound repair. The problem is what the cell does next. It stays alive and metabolically busy and releases a mixture of inflammatory cytokines such as interleukin six and eight, enzymes that break down matrix, and growth factors. This secretory profile, the SASP, was characterised in human cells grown in the laboratory after DNA damage. In living human skin, the evidence is observational. Skin samples from older people contain more cells carrying the senescence marker p16, in both the epidermis and the dermis, and fibroblasts, keratinocytes and melanocytes can all become senescent. Researchers also caution that no single marker identifies a senescent cell with certainty, so counts depend on the marker chosen.

body.en: In a Dutch cohort, people with more p16-positive cells in sun-protected arm skin had more ageing-type elastic fibres, more facial wrinkles and looked older, after allowing for their actual age. The epidermal p16-positive cells were mostly melanocytes. The study was publicly funded; one co-author worked for Unilever.

detail.en: Waaijer et al., 2016 — 178 adults aged 45–81, Leiden Longevity Study, sun-protected arm biopsies

means.en: Senescent-cell burden in human skin tracks visible ageing, even in skin that sees little sun.

doesNot.en: It does not show that senescent cells cause wrinkles, or that removing them would reverse any. One observational cohort shows an association.

body.en: Senescence research mixes human tissue, mice and cultured cells. For the ageing dermis the four answers point in different directions, which is why they belong in separate sentences.

note.en: Skin collagen falls with age. Aged human dermis shows more fibroblast MMP-1 and fragmented collagen; in culture, fragmentation raises MMP-1 further. That senescent cells drive this in living skin is plausible, not shown.
p16-positive cells rise with age and track with wrinkles and perceived age
Clearing p16-positive cells, or giving senolytic drugs, extends healthy lifespan in mice. Skin was checked only for safety, and clearing these cells during healing slowed wound closure.

Small pilots measuring tissue markers. One exploratory randomized trial of topical rapamycin (36 enrolled, 19 dropped out) lowered skin p16, and clinical change was only described. No adequately sized trial with clinical skin-ageing outcomes was found (September 2026).

callout.en: A mouse lifespan result is not a skin treatment.

title.en: The levers with trials behind them.

body.en: Two ways of protecting or rebuilding the dermal matrix have randomized human trials. In a community trial of 903 adults, daily sunscreen for four and a half years slowed photoageing compared with discretionary use (GRADE B). Topical tretinoin improves photoageing consistently across randomized trials, and the Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide rates topical retinoids first-line, GRADE A. Retinol improved fine wrinkles in very old skin in a small trial (C), and within a week it raised collagen synthesis and lowered MMPs in biopsies of aged human skin.

points.en: Daily sunscreen: one large RCT (B)
Topical retinoids for photoageing: GRADE A
Senolytics for skin: no clinical-outcome trials yet

blocks.sourceNote: Hughes 2013 · Sitohang 2022 · Kafi 2007 · Varani 2000 · Fisher 2002 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 5

body.en: A publicly funded Australian trial of 903 adults: daily sunscreen meant about a quarter less skin ageing over four and a half years.
Consistent randomized trials for tretinoin in photoaged skin; the guide's GRADE A. Retinol has smaller trials, including one in very old skin.
Biomarker pilots only, so far. They sit below the levers that already have outcome data.

audioScript.en: Set the senescence story beside the interventions that have been tested in people. In Nambour, Australia, a publicly funded trial randomised 903 adults to daily or discretionary sunscreen, and over four and a half years skin ageing was about a quarter lower with daily use. Topical tretinoin has a run of randomised trials in photoaged skin that agree with one another, and the Aesthetic and Regenerative Endocrinology guide rates topical retinoids first-line, grade A. Retinol has smaller trials, including one in residents in their late eighties whose fine wrinkling improved and whose biopsies showed more procollagen. Both levers protect or rebuild the dermal matrix that ultraviolet light and, it is thought, the SASP erode, and both have human outcome data. Senolytics for skin have no such data yet. Keep that order in mind when a patient asks what actually works.

audioScript.en: Consider a fifty-eight-year-old patient, fictional and built from this lesson's evidence. She has read that senolytic supplements clear so-called zombie cells and reverse skin ageing, and she asks whether to start one she found online. She does not wear sunscreen every day. Three facts frame the conversation. Senescent cells really do accumulate in human skin, and their number tracks with wrinkles and with how old a person looks. The evidence that clearing them helps comes from mice, and the human studies so far are small pilots measuring markers in tissue. Daily sunscreen and topical retinoids, by contrast, have randomised trials with visible skin outcomes. The Aesthetic and Regenerative Endocrinology guide advises keeping senolytics within clinical trials. Decide what you say first.

advisor.en: You explain the difference between mouse and human evidence, reinforce daily sunscreen, and suggest a prescriber for a retinoid or if she wants to explore a trial.

summary.en: Cutaneous 11β-HSD1 and local cortisol conversion; clinical triage of hypercortisolemia versus cosmetic 'cortisol face'; estrogen withdrawal kinetics and postmenopausal collagen loss; systemic and topical hormone therapy boundaries; pathognomonic skin signs of endocrine syndromes.

objective.en: By the end, you can differentiate cutaneous manifestations of systemic endocrine disorders from localized hormonal aging, appraising the clinical limitations and risks of hormone replacement in skin health.

units.tutorContext: Module 2 separates local hormonal skin biology from systemic endocrine disease and keeps four registers apart (mechanism, human evidence, regulatory status, open question). Cortisol: skin expresses an HPA-like axis (CRH, POMC/ACTH) and regenerates cortisol via 11β-HSD1 in keratinocytes and fibroblasts; activity higher in aged and photo-exposed skin, set independently of blood levels (mechanism, D). Only human 11β-HSD1 skin RCT: 28-person pilot in type 2 diabetes, primary outcome missed, exploratory faster wound closure (C); investigational, no FDA approval, no skin-ageing trial registered (24 Sep 2026). Endocrine Society 2008: best discriminators of Cushing's = easy bruising, facial plethora, proximal myopathy, reddish-purple striae >1 cm; facial fullness, dorsocervical fat pad, weight gain, acne, hirsutism, fatigue are common/less discriminating; drug history first (incl. skin-bleaching creams, injections); endogenous incidence 2–3 per million/yr; commonest cause iatrogenic; test multiple progressive features; against widespread testing and random serum cortisol; abnormal → endocrinologist. Estrogen: ERα/ERβ/GPER in skin; topical estradiol raises collagen in sun-protected not photoaged skin (D); collagen and thickness fall ~1–2%/yr after menopause tracking years since menopause (D; the guide's '30% in 5 years' is a review figure not found in primary abstracts). Systemic HT: small RCTs raise skin thickness/collagen (C); largest RCT (n=485, 48 wk) and 4-year KEEPS found no wrinkle difference (B); guide grades B, NAMS Level II, course C for structural gains. US (Feb 2026): MHT approved for hot flashes, vulvovaginal/GSM symptoms, bone loss (some products); 2025–26 label changes removed CV/breast/dementia statements from boxed warning; skin never an indication. NAMS 2022: favourable <60 or within 10 years for symptoms/bone; compounded bioidentical HT insufficient evidence. OTC 'hormone creams' = unapproved drugs (21 CFR 310.530). Skin care with better evidence: daily sunscreen (RCT n=903, B); tretinoin cream FDA-approved adjunct for fine wrinkles. UK (checked 25 Sep 2026): HRT products are prescription-only medicines licensed for oestrogen-deficiency symptoms and, for some, osteoporosis prevention (Evorel, Sandrena SmPCs); skin is not a licensed use; compounded 'bioidentical' hormones are unlicensed medicines (MHRA GN14 puts a licensed product first); UK topical tretinoin on the medicines compendium is acne-only. Red flags → referral, never diagnosis by the aesthetic clinician: rapid hirsutism/virilization (tumour ~0.2%, >half malignant) urgent; generalised hyperpigmentation in creases/scars/mucosa with illness (adrenal insufficiency) urgent; Cushing's discriminators, MEN1 angiofibromas (88% of MEN1, not in tuberous sclerosis), Carney complex (lip/eyelid/canthal lentigines, blue naevi, myxomas; cardiac myxomas >50% of deaths), MEN2A interscapular lichen amyloidosis (RET 634) → endocrine referral. Never give doses, regimens or product sourcing; adapt 'what you do next' to prescriber, clinical staff or advisor without changing facts. No CME credit is currently offered.

videoTranscript.en: Most skin changes you see are ageing or lifestyle. A few are the first visible sign of endocrine disease. In three lessons you will separate them: what local and systemic hormones do to skin, what hormone therapy can and cannot do for it, and which signs belong with an endocrinologist. Picture the skin as a small endocrine organ with its own stress axis. Skin cells make CRH and ACTH, the same signals that drive the adrenal glands, and they carry the receptors to respond to them. They also carry an enzyme called eleven beta HSD one, which turns inactive cortisone back into active cortisol inside the cell. In human skin samples that enzyme works harder with age and in sun-exposed skin, and it sets local cortisol independently of the level in the blood. Cortisol slows collagen production in dermal fibroblasts, and mice bred without the enzyme kept their dermal thickness as they aged. Hold all of this in the mechanism register. It comes from biopsies, cultured cells and mice, and it says nothing yet about how a patient's face will age.

title.en: The skin regenerates its own cortisol.

body.en: Skin expresses the machinery of a local stress axis, including CRH and POMC with its product ACTH. Keratinocytes and dermal fibroblasts also carry 11β-HSD1, the enzyme that turns inactive cortisone back into active cortisol inside the cell. In human skin samples its activity is higher with age and in sun-exposed skin, and local cortisol availability is set independently of blood levels. Cortisol slows collagen production in dermal fibroblasts, and mice lacking the enzyme kept their dermal thickness with age.

points.en: Local axis: CRH, POMC and ACTH are made in skin
11β-HSD1 regenerates cortisol inside skin cells
Mechanism register: human samples, cultured cells and mice

blocks.sourceNote: Slominski & Wortsman 2000 · Tiganescu 2011, 2013 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 8

body.en: Skin makes CRH and POMC-derived ACTH and carries their receptors, a field-restricted copy of the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis.
11β-HSD1 converts cortisone to cortisol in keratinocytes and fibroblasts. In human skin samples its activity rises with age and with sun exposure.
Cortisol slows collagen synthesis in fibroblasts, and knockout mice kept their dermal thickness as they aged. Whether this drives visible ageing in people has not been tested.

callout.en: Local cortisol is set inside the skin, independently of blood levels, so a systemic cortisol test does not measure it.

body.en: Cushing's syndrome shares most of its features with ordinary weight gain, poor sleep and stress. The Endocrine Society's diagnostic guideline separates the few that discriminate from the many that are common. Before you see its verdicts, sort these eight.

blocks.sourceNote: Endocrine Society guideline, Nieman 2008, Table 1 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 8

note.en: Bruises without an obvious injury
A persistently red, full-blooded complexion
Trouble rising from a chair or climbing stairs
Reddish-purple and wider than 1 cm
A rounder face than a year ago
Gradual gain over several years
New or persistent
Tired, sleeping badly

callout.en: Few features of Cushing's syndrome are unique. Some discriminate far better than others.

prompt.en: Tap where each feature belongs.

why.en: One of the four features the guideline lists as best discriminating, particularly bruising with no obvious trauma.
Listed among the best discriminators. Most of the four have low sensitivity, so their absence does not exclude the syndrome.
Proximal myopathy is one of the four; ask about stairs and getting up from a low chair.
The guideline singles out striae that are reddish-purple and wider than 1 cm.
The guideline lists facial fullness, like the dorsocervical fat pad, among features that are common in the general population. A round face alone is a weak signal.
Common and less discriminatory on its own; many features of cortisol excess are shared with ordinary obesity.
Both sit on the guideline's common, less discriminatory list; persistent hirsutism more often points to androgen excess (lesson 2.3).
Fatigue, insomnia and poor concentration are common and less discriminatory.

done.en: Eight sorted. Four features discriminate: easy bruising, facial plethora, proximal weakness and wide reddish-purple striae. A round face on its own is a weak signal.

title.en: Rare, and usually from a prescription.

body.en: Endogenous Cushing's syndrome is uncommon: European population studies put it at two to three new cases per million people a year. The commonest cause of Cushing's syndrome is iatrogenic, from glucocorticoids given as medicine. The Endocrine Society therefore asks for a drug history first, covering tablets, inhalers, injections and creams, including skin-bleaching products, and recommends testing when features are multiple and progressive.

label.en: new cases of endogenous Cushing's syndrome per million people per year (European population studies)

detail.en: As cited in the Endocrine Society diagnostic guideline, 2008

means.en: A round, puffy face in an aesthetic clinic is almost always something other than Cushing's syndrome, and when cortisol excess is real it most often comes from a glucocorticoid the patient is already using.

doesNot.en: It does not mean you can dismiss it. The guideline recommends testing when discriminating features are multiple and progressive or unusual for age, and some groups, such as people with poorly controlled diabetes, carry a higher rate.

title.en: Reassure the many, refer the few.

body.en: When a patient asks about 'cortisol face', start with the drug history: steroid creams, skin-lighteners, herbal tonics and injections. Then look for the discriminating features. Without them, the Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide reads most puffiness as sleep, alcohol, salt and fluid, and the Endocrine Society recommends against widespread testing. With them, especially when they are progressing, the next step is formal testing and an endocrinologist. A cortisol supplement or a consumer cortisol panel answers the wrong question.

body.en: Glucocorticoids hide in skin-bleaching creams, herbal tonics and joint or nerve injections. The guideline asks for that history before any cortisol test.
Easy bruising, a plethoric face, proximal weakness and wide reddish-purple striae are the features that shift the odds.
First-line tests are urine free cortisol, late-night salivary cortisol or an overnight dexamethasone suppression test, ordered by a prescriber; an abnormal result goes to an endocrinologist.

audioScript.en: Here is how that plays out when a patient asks about cortisol face. Begin with a drug history, because the commonest cause of cortisol excess is a glucocorticoid someone is already using. The guideline names the easy ones to miss, such as skin-bleaching creams, herbal tonics, and joint or nerve injections. Then look for the four features that shift the odds, meaning easy bruising, a plethoric face, weakness in the hips and shoulders, and wide reddish-purple striae. Without them, the Aesthetic and Regenerative Endocrinology guide reads most puffiness as sleep, alcohol, salt and fluid, and the Endocrine Society advises against testing everyone. With them, and especially when they are progressing, the patient needs formal testing and an endocrinologist. A cortisol supplement or a mail-order saliva panel answers the wrong question.

prescriber.en: If discriminating features are present, arrange one of the guideline's first-line tests or refer directly to endocrinology, and document the drug history, including creams and injections. An abnormal result goes to an endocrinologist.

clinical-staff.en: Record any steroid creams, skin-lighteners or injections the patient mentions, note bruising or wide purple striae you see, and bring it to the prescriber before the next treatment.

advisor.en: Do not recommend 'cortisol-lowering' supplements or consumer cortisol kits. If a patient describes easy bruising, muscle weakness or new wide purple stretch marks, point them to a prescriber.

body.en: Skin carries estrogen receptors (ERα, ERβ and the membrane receptor GPER) in both sun-protected and sun-damaged sites. In postmenopausal women, two weeks of topical estradiol raised collagen production in sun-protected hip skin; photoaged facial skin showed no such response. After menopause, small biopsy studies found skin collagen and thickness falling year by year, following years since menopause more closely than age. That is mechanism and natural history. What hormone therapy does to a face is a separate question.

title.en: A collagen signal, with a limit

audioScript.en: Estrogen is the hormone the guide says dominates the visible ageing of women's skin, so start with what it does in the dermis. Skin carries estrogen receptors in sun-protected and sun-damaged sites alike. In a vehicle-controlled study, two weeks of topical estradiol raised collagen production in the hip skin of postmenopausal women; in photoaged forearm and facial skin, the same treatment made no measurable difference. Small biopsy studies from the nineteen eighties and nineties found that skin collagen and thickness fall after menopause, and that the fall follows years since the last period more closely than birthdays. Keep two questions apart as you go. One is what estrogen does in the dermis. The other is whether giving it changes how a face ages, and those answers come from different trials.

alt.en: Two panels of dermis: in sun-protected skin, receptor-bearing cells lay down new collagen; in sun-damaged skin, the same cells sit among fragmented, clumped fibres with no new collagen.

title.en: One to two per cent a year.

body.en: In small biopsy studies of postmenopausal women, skin collagen content and skin thickness fell by about 1–2% a year, in step with bone mass, and followed years since menopause more than age. Reviews, and the Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide, quote a steeper early loss of up to 30% in the first five years. That figure traces to the same small studies, and a check of their abstracts in September 2026 did not find it stated.

blocks.sourceNote: Brincat 1985, 1987 · Affinito 1999 · Thornton 2013

label.en: fall in skin collagen content and thickness per year after menopause (small biopsy studies)

detail.en: Brincat et al., 1987 — in parallel with bone mass

means.en: Estrogen withdrawal is a measurable contributor to dermal thinning, and it follows the menopause clock rather than age alone.

doesNot.en: It does not show that hormone therapy restores a younger-looking face. These are small observational studies, mostly of non-facial skin; the treatment trials come next.

body.en: Hormone therapy has two kinds of trial behind it. Small trials measure the dermis; larger trials measure the face. They point in different directions, so read them separately. The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide grades the skin benefit B; the North American Menopause Society rates the same evidence 'limited or inconsistent'. This course grades the structural gains C and teaches the negative wrinkle trials alongside them.

blocks.sourceNote: Maheux 1994 · Sauerbronn 2000 · Phillips 2008 · Owen 2016 · Pivazyan 2023 · Creidi 1994 · Ashcroft 1999 · NAMS 2022

label.en: Systemic HT · skin thickness and collagen

note.en: Two small RCTs (60 and 41 women) measured hip and upper-arm skin
485 women for 48 weeks on low-dose therapy; a four-year trial in recently menopausal women also found no difference
Small studies, some non-randomized, varying widely; its authors do not propose hormone therapy as a skin treatment
One 24-week RCT improved thickness and fine lines; a biopsy study found no collagen response in photoaged facial skin
A small randomized study in healthy older adults

callout.en: A thicker dermis on biopsy and a younger-looking face are different outcomes. Ask which one a trial measured.

title.en: Symptoms and bone. Skin is a bystander.

body.en: In the US, as of February 2026, FDA-approved menopausal hormone therapy is for moderate-to-severe hot flashes, vaginal and vulvar symptoms and, for some products, preventing bone loss. FDA's 2025–26 labeling changes removed cardiovascular, breast-cancer and dementia statements from the boxed warning; skin did not become an indication. The North American Menopause Society's 2022 statement finds benefit outweighs risk for bothersome symptoms and bone protection when therapy starts before 60 or within 10 years of menopause, and finds insufficient evidence for compounded 'bioidentical' hormones. Under US rules an over-the-counter 'hormone cream' is an unapproved drug. For the skin itself, daily sunscreen has a large randomized trial behind it, and one tretinoin cream is FDA-approved as an adjunct for fine facial wrinkles.

points.en: Indications: hot flashes, genitourinary symptoms, bone
Low-dose vaginal estrogen for GSM: the one estrogen-for-tissue use
For the skin itself: daily sunscreen and a retinoid

blocks.sourceNote: FDA, 10 Nov 2025 and 12 Feb 2026 · 21 CFR 310.530 · NAMS 2022, 2020 · Manson 2013 · Hughes 2013 · Renova label · UK: Evorel and Sandrena SmPCs, MHRA Guidance Note 14, medicines compendium (checked 25 Sep 2026)

body.en: In the US, hot flashes, vaginal and vulvar symptoms and, for some products, bone loss. The 2025–26 label changes did not add skin.

For bothersome symptoms and bone, when started before 60 or within ten years of menopause, per the 2022 position statement. The large WHI trials do not support hormone therapy for preventing chronic disease.

title.en: What to decline, and what to offer

body.en: Compounded 'bioidentical' preparations lack efficacy and safety data, and over-the-counter 'hormone creams' are unapproved drugs under US rules. Daily sunscreen and a prescription retinoid have better evidence for the skin.

audioScript.en: Where does that leave hormone therapy for skin? In the United States, as of February 2026, the approved uses of menopausal hormone therapy are hot flashes, vaginal and vulvar symptoms, and for some products the prevention of bone loss. In late 2025 the FDA asked manufacturers to remove heart, breast cancer and dementia statements from the boxed warning, and it approved the first revised labels in February 2026. Skin still appears nowhere among the uses. The menopause society's 2022 position statement finds the balance favourable for symptoms and bone when therapy starts before sixty or within ten years of menopause, and it finds too little evidence for compounded bioidentical hormones. Low-dose vaginal estrogen for genitourinary symptoms is the one use aimed at the tissue itself. For the face, daily sunscreen and a prescription retinoid carry better evidence than any hormone. Treat symptoms on their merits, and count any skin change as a bonus.

prescriber.en: Prescribe hormone therapy for its labeled indications and the position statement's timing, and record that skin was discussed only as a secondary effect. Do not prescribe systemic or topical estrogen for wrinkles alone, and prefer licensed products (FDA-approved in the US) to compounded 'bioidentical' preparations.

clinical-staff.en: If a patient asks for 'hormones for my skin', ask about hot flashes, sleep and vaginal symptoms, record what she says, and route those symptoms to the prescriber. The skin concern stays with skin-directed care.

advisor.en: In the US, a cream sold as containing estrogen for the face is regulated as a drug, and compounded 'bioidentical' products lack efficacy and safety data. Menopausal symptoms are a conversation for a prescriber; sun protection is advice you can give.

text.en: In the UK, as of September 2026, HRT products such as estradiol patches and gel are prescription-only medicines licensed for oestrogen-deficiency symptoms and, for some, for preventing osteoporosis in women at high risk of fracture; skin is not among their uses. A compounded 'bioidentical' hormone is an unlicensed medicine in the UK, and MHRA guidance puts a licensed product first when one can meet the need. On the UK medicines compendium, topical tretinoin appears only in acne treatments.

In the EU, the harmonised core product information for HRT (CMDh, December 2025) lists oestrogen-deficiency symptoms after menopause, osteoporosis prevention and vaginal atrophy as its indications; skin is not an indication. EU cosmetics law prohibits oestrogens, progestogens and tretinoin in cosmetic products (Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009, Annex II), and anti-wrinkle products containing tretinoin marketed as cosmetics are illegal cosmetics.

In Portugal, as of September 2026, the estradiol HRT products Estreva gel and Estrofem tablets are authorised for symptoms of oestrogen deficiency in postmenopausal women. The topical tretinoin product Ketrel cream is authorised and prescription-only on INFARMED's database, with indications for acne (except acne rosacea) and keratinisation disorders.

In Brazil, as of September 2026, estradiol for menopausal hormone therapy is registered and the Oestrogel label covers menopausal symptoms and prevention of postmenopausal osteoporosis, not skin ageing, while the Vitacid label for topical tretinoin names cutaneous photoageing as well as acne vulgaris. The Federal Council of Medicine (CFM) bars physicians from using hormones, in any formulation, except in diagnosed deficiencies where replacement shows evidence of scientifically proven benefit (Resolution 1.999/2012), and from prescribing hormones marketed as 'bioidentical' or 'nano' without proof of superiority (Resolution 2.333/2023).

In the UAE, the Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE), the federal regulator of medical products since Federal Decree-Law 28/2023, registers estradiol products as Prescription Only Medicines, for example Oestrogel gel (since 11 November 2021). The EDE register lists therapeutic categories rather than indications, so it does not show whether any UAE label includes a skin indication (25 September 2026). Under the medicines law, Federal Decree-Law 38 of 2024, a compounding pharmacy may not compound products that are essentially copies of EDE-approved products unless no commercially available product can deliver the expected benefit to the patient.

prompt.en: A 52-year-old with no hot flashes, no sleep disturbance and no vaginal symptoms asks for estrogen 'to stop my face ageing'. What does the evidence support?

text.en: Estrogen rebuilds collagen, so hormone therapy is a reasonable anti-ageing choice.

why.en: That is the mechanism talking. Small trials show thicker skin, the largest trials found no difference in wrinkles, and skin is not an approved indication.

text.en: A compounded 'bioidentical' estrogen face cream avoids the risks of systemic therapy.

why.en: Compounded 'bioidentical' preparations lack efficacy and safety data and carry quality concerns; the menopause society says preference alone should not justify them.

text.en: Skin alone is not a reason to start hormone therapy; offer skin-directed care such as daily sunscreen and a retinoid, and revisit therapy if menopausal symptoms appear.

why.en: Correct. Symptoms decide hormone therapy. For skin, daily sunscreen has a large trial behind it and one tretinoin cream is FDA-approved as an adjunct for fine wrinkles.

feedback.en: Symptoms decide hormone therapy; skin gets skin-directed care.

title.en: Some syndromes show on the skin first.

body.en: A handful of inherited endocrine syndromes appear on the skin before the glands declare themselves. In multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN1), multiple facial angiofibromas and collagenomas are common. In Carney complex, lentigines on the lips, eyelids and canthi, blue naevi and small skin myxomas sit alongside myxomas of the heart and cortisol-secreting adrenal disease. In MEN2A, an itchy, rippled, pigmented plaque between the shoulder blades can precede medullary thyroid cancer.

points.en: MEN1: facial angiofibromas, collagenomas
Carney complex: lip and eyelid lentigines, myxomas
MEN2A: lichen amyloidosis between the shoulder blades

blocks.sourceNote: Darling 1997 · Kirschner 2000 · Correa 2015 · Stanescu 2024 · Lause 2017 · the guide's inherited-syndromes chapter

body.en: Loss of the tumour suppressor menin. Multiple facial angiofibromas, identical to those of tuberous sclerosis, and truncal collagenomas.
Inactivating variants in PRKAR1A, the regulatory subunit of protein kinase A. Lentigines, blue naevi and myxomas of skin and heart, with Cushing's syndrome from the adrenal.
Activating RET variants, most often at codon 634 when the skin is involved. Cutaneous lichen amyloidosis over the upper back, often found before the thyroid cancer.

audioScript.en: Some endocrine syndromes are written on the skin years before the glands give them away. In multiple endocrine neoplasia type one, most patients in one careful series had several facial angiofibromas, the same lesions seen in tuberous sclerosis, along with collagenomas on the trunk. In Carney complex, usually caused by inactivating variants in the PRKAR1A gene, freckle-like lentigines cluster on the lips, eyelids and the corners of the eyes, alongside blue naevi and small skin myxomas. The same patients can develop myxomas in the heart and cortisol-secreting adrenal disease. In MEN two A, an itchy, rippled, darkened patch between the shoulder blades, called cutaneous lichen amyloidosis, can appear long before medullary thyroid cancer. Each of these is a referral finding, and none of them is yours to diagnose alone.

body.en: In a consecutive series of 32 people with MEN1 examined at the US National Institutes of Health, 88% had multiple facial angiofibromas and 72% had collagenomas. The angiofibromas were clinically and histologically identical to those of tuberous sclerosis. The authors concluded that angiofibromas in someone without tuberous sclerosis call for biochemical testing for MEN1.

blocks.sourceNote: Darling et al., Arch Dermatol 1997

label.en: of 32 people with MEN1 had multiple facial angiofibromas

detail.en: Darling et al., 1997 — collagenomas in 72%

means.en: Multiple facial angiofibromas are common in MEN1 and can be its first visible sign; in someone without tuberous sclerosis they are a reason for endocrine testing, whatever the cosmetic plan.

doesNot.en: It does not mean a single facial papule is MEN1. This is one small referral-centre series, and angiofibromas have other causes, tuberous sclerosis above all.

body.en: Most endocrine skin signs you meet come from common disease. New generalised darkening, strongest in skin creases, scars, mucosa and sun-exposed skin, can signal primary adrenal insufficiency, which can turn into a life-threatening crisis. Hirsutism that appears fast, keeps progressing, or comes with a deepening voice or clitoromegaly makes an androgen-secreting tumour more likely. Velvety dark plaques of acanthosis nigricans track insulin resistance, pretibial myxoedema points to Graves' disease, and cold, dry skin suggests hypothyroidism.

points.en: Darkening in creases, scars and gums: adrenal insufficiency
Rapid hirsutism or virilization: exclude a tumour
Acanthosis, pretibial plaques, dry cool skin: metabolic and thyroid

blocks.sourceNote: Endocrine Society guidelines: Bornstein 2016, Martin 2018 · Lause 2017 · the guide's ch. 5 referral list

body.en: The hyperpigmentation of primary adrenal insufficiency favours sun-exposed skin, creases, mucosa and scars. In an acutely ill patient the guideline recommends testing, and a suspected crisis is treated before results return.
Rapid onset or progression of hirsutism, or signs of virilization, raise the likelihood of an androgen-secreting tumour and call for prompt referral.
Acanthosis nigricans reflects hyperinsulinaemia; pretibial myxoedema reflects thyrotropin-receptor stimulation in Graves' disease; hypothyroid skin is cold and dry.

audioScript.en: Most of the endocrine skin signs you will actually meet come from common conditions. New, generalised darkening, most obvious in skin creases such as the palms, in scars, on the gums and on sun-exposed skin, can be the sign of primary adrenal insufficiency. In a patient who is also unwell, the Endocrine Society recommends testing, and a suspected adrenal crisis is treated before the results come back, because delay raises the risk of death. Hirsutism that arrives quickly, keeps progressing, or comes with a deeper voice or clitoromegaly makes an androgen-secreting tumour more likely and calls for prompt referral. Velvety dark plaques in the neck folds track insulin resistance. Firm plaques on the shins point to Graves' disease, and cold, dry, coarse skin suggests an underactive thyroid. The skin shows you which door to knock on.

label.en: Coarse chin and chest hair over four months; her voice has deepened

why.en: Hyperpigmentation with systemic symptoms suggests primary adrenal insufficiency; the guideline recommends testing in unwell patients and treating a suspected crisis without waiting for results.

label.en: Wide purple abdominal striae, easy bruising, trouble climbing stairs

why.en: Several discriminating features together: the guideline recommends testing for Cushing's syndrome, and the guide lists it for prompt endocrine referral.

label.en: Several facial angiofibromas, no tuberous sclerosis; her father had parathyroid surgery

why.en: Angiofibromas outside tuberous sclerosis call for biochemical testing for MEN1, and a relative with parathyroid disease strengthens the case.

label.en: Itchy, rippled brown patch between the shoulder blades; an aunt had thyroid cancer

why.en: Interscapular lichen amyloidosis clusters with RET variants in MEN2A and can precede medullary thyroid cancer; with that family history it needs endocrine and genetic assessment.

label.en: Puffy face after late nights; no bruising, striae or weakness

why.en: Facial fullness alone is a common, weakly discriminating feature, and the guideline advises against testing everyone. Reassess if discriminating features appear.

label.en: A few coarse hairs on the chin only; regular periods

why.en: The Endocrine Society suggests against androgen testing in women with regular cycles and unwanted local hair without an abnormal hirsutism score. Hair removal is a reasonable cosmetic choice.

done.en: Seven routed. Two need urgent assessment, three need an endocrine referral, and two can stay with skin-directed care.

label.en: Proceed with the laser: lentigines are benign and she has a deadline.

why.en: The spots may well be benign. Their distribution, the eyelid papule and the family history are what matter, and together they flag a possible syndrome.

why.en: Right. Canthal and lip lentigines with a possible myxoma and a family cardiac tumour fit Carney complex, where early echocardiographic screening matters. You route; the specialist diagnoses.

label.en: Order a cortisol test to check for Cushing's before deciding.

why.en: Cortisol excess is one feature of Carney complex, but a single test neither assesses the syndrome nor its cardiac risk. Referral comes first.

followUp.en: Then explain why in plain words: the pattern of spots, the eyelid bump and her father's history together deserve a specialist's look, and the laser can wait.

audioScript.en: Consider a fictional patient, built from this lesson's evidence. She is twenty-nine and wants the freckles on her lips and at the corners of her eyes lasered before her wedding. While you examine her you notice a soft, skin-coloured bump on one eyelid. She mentions that her father had a heart tumour removed in his thirties. Pigmented spots at the corners of the eyes are seen in Carney complex and Peutz–Jeghers syndrome, and small skin myxomas favour the eyelids and ears. In Carney complex, tumours of the heart cause more than half of the deaths, which is why screening matters once the diagnosis is suspected. The laser itself may be harmless. The question is what the skin is telling you. Choose your first move.

prescriber.en: Document the lentigines, the eyelid lesion and the family history, refer to endocrinology or clinical genetics, and leave echocardiography and testing to that assessment. Defer the laser until then.

clinical-staff.en: Hold the booking, photograph with consent if your setting allows, record the family history in her words, and bring it to the prescriber the same day.

advisor.en: Explain that the pattern of spots is worth a specialist's look before any cosmetic treatment, and point her to a prescriber; do not suggest a product to fade them.

prompt.en: Closing Module 2: which statement keeps mechanism, evidence, regulation and the open question apart?

text.en: Estrogen raises dermal collagen, so hormone therapy is indicated for skin ageing.

why.en: That blends mechanism into indication. The collagen effect is real in small trials; the approved uses are symptoms and bone.
