body.en: Researchers made test purchases of semaglutide from illegal online pharmacies and analysed what arrived. The three vials that were delivered were all judged probably substandard or falsified: purity measured 7.7–14.4% against the 99% printed on the label, peptide content ran 29–39% above the labelled amount, and endotoxin was found in every vial, although none grew microorganisms.

blocks.sourceNote: Ashraf et al., J Med Internet Res 2024 · Peptide Pocket Guide

label.en: measured purity of online semaglutide vials labelled 99%

detail.en: Ashraf et al., J Med Internet Res 2024 · three delivered vials · endotoxin detected in all three

means.en: Purity printed on a label can be wildly wrong, and a vial that grows nothing can still carry endotoxin. Independent testing found what the paperwork hid.

doesNot.en: Three vials of one drug give no market-wide failure rate, and semaglutide is outside the skin-peptide shelf. It documents the gap between claim and content for one product; it does not measure research peptides as a class.

title.en: Research use only is a label, and never a route.

body.en: In the US, 'not for use in humans' labelling lets a supplier ship an investigational drug for laboratory or in-vitro research, and obliges the shipper to check that is how it will be used. FDA reads intended use from claims, marketing and the circumstances of sale, so the disclaimer changes nothing about a vial sold with injection instructions. A certificate cannot turn such a product into a pharmaceutical.

points.en: The label permits laboratory research only
Intended use is read from how a product is sold
A certificate cannot convert a research product

blocks.sourceNote: 21 CFR 312.160 · 21 CFR 201.128 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 3 · Peptide Pocket Guide, regulatory chapter

body.en: The US rule lets a supplier ship a drug for laboratory or in-vitro research when the label says it is not for use in humans.
FDA reads what a product is for from its claims, marketing and how it is sold, so a disclaimer on a vial sold for injection carries no weight.
However clean, it cannot supply sterility, manufacturing standards or a lawful route.

audioScript.en: Research use only sounds like a category. In law it works as a shipping permission. The US rule lets a supplier send an investigational drug for laboratory or test-tube work if the label says it must stay out of people, and the shipper is meant to confirm that is how it will be used. FDA judges what a product is for by how it is marketed and sold, so a disclaimer on a vial offered with injection instructions carries no weight. The Hormonaly guides say it plainly. Research use only is not a clinical pathway. A certificate of analysis, however clean, cannot convert that vial into a pharmaceutical, because sterility, manufacturing standards and a lawful route are all still missing. Whatever your role, treat these products as outside clinical care, and write down exactly what you were told.

prescriber.en: Do not prescribe, supply, supervise or recommend a research-use-only product, and do not read its certificate as permission. Record the product, lot and supplier the patient names, and your advice to stop.

clinical-staff.en: If a patient brings a research-use-only vial or its certificate, record the product name, lot and supplier exactly as printed, do not handle or administer it, and tell the prescriber the same day.

advisor.en: You can explain what a certificate does and does not show. You cannot vouch for a research product, and anyone injecting one should see a prescriber.

text.en: In the EU, a product is a medicine by presentation (presented as treating or preventing disease) or by function (restoring, correcting or modifying physiological functions by a pharmacological, immunological or metabolic action), and where it could be both a medicine and another regulated product, medicines law applies (Directive 2001/83/EC, Articles 1(2) and 2(2)). The Directive's research exclusion covers medicinal products intended for research and development trials (Article 3(3)).

In Portugal, a medicine is any substance or combination of substances presented as having properties for treating or preventing disease in human beings or its symptoms, or which may be used in or administered to human beings to make a medical diagnosis or to restore, correct or modify physiological functions by exerting a pharmacological, immunological or metabolic action (Estatuto do Medicamento). Making, selling, supplying or administering medicines without the required authorisations or registrations is an administrative offence punishable by a fine from €2,000 up to 15% of turnover or €180,000, whichever is lower.

In Brazil, ANVISA stated on 2 July 2026 that some injectable peptides are not regularised in any category (food, medicine, cosmetic or food supplement) and so are illegal for any health use, including aesthetic use. ANVISA also stated in July 2026 that an investigational medicine is used only in authorised clinical research.

In the UAE, Federal Decree-Law 38 of 2024 has, since 2 January 2025, barred importing, distributing, possessing, selling, displaying or using any medical product without a marketing approval from the Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE), the federal regulator of medical products since Federal Decree-Law 28/2023. In Dubai, the DHA prohibits using any peptide product intended for research use on humans, or for therapeutic purposes outside an approved study or clinical trial, and bars facilities from buying peptide products from websites, social media or unverifiable suppliers (29 July 2026). In Abu Dhabi, the DoH's compounding standard (August 2026) prohibits compounding from unapproved or unknown-source substances, or from substances not on the DoH Registry for Compounded Substances, unless the DoH permits it.

title.en: Selling and advertising peptides outside the US.

body.en: Outside the US, whether a peptide is regulated as a medicine turns on what is claimed for it and on what it is and does, not on the category a seller chooses, and a medicine without a marketing authorisation may not be sold, supplied or advertised. Advertising a prescription-only medicine to the public is prohibited, or needs the regulator's prior approval.

points.en: Medicine or not: what is claimed, and what it is and does
No marketing authorisation: no sale, supply or advertising
Prescription-only: public advertising banned or approved first

body.en: Regulators look at what is claimed for a product and at what it is and does. A research-use label or a cosmetic box does not settle it.
A medicine with no marketing authorisation may not be sold, supplied or advertised, whatever the label calls it.
Advertising a prescription-only medicine to the public is prohibited or needs the regulator's approval first, and social media counts.

audioScript.en: Selling a peptide outside the United States starts with one question, whether the product is a medicine, and regulators answer it from the product itself. They look at what is claimed for it and at what it is and does, so a research-use label or a cosmetic box settles nothing. A medicine without a marketing authorisation may not be sold, supplied or advertised. Advertising a prescription-only medicine to the public is prohibited, or needs the regulator's approval first, and that covers posts on social media by clinics and influencers. The details differ from country to country, so check the rules for your own jurisdiction, shown with this moment, and date what you find.

text.en: In the UK, MHRA decides whether a product is a medicine from its claims, including websites and social media, and from its form and the way it is used. A medicine with no UK marketing authorisation may not be sold, supplied or advertised. MHRA classes injectable melanotan products as medicines, and its largest seizure of unlicensed weight-loss medicines, in May 2026, included peptide products. Prescription-only medicines may not be advertised to the public at all: a clinic may promote 'treatment for lines and wrinkles' without naming the medicine, and in February 2026 the UK advertising regulator ruled that influencer posts tagging a weight-loss injection were adverts for a prescription-only medicine. GMC guidance requires doctors to examine a patient physically before prescribing an injectable cosmetic medicine.

In the EU, member states must prohibit any advertising of a medicine that has no marketing authorisation, and any advertising of prescription-only medicines to the general public, where advertising includes any inducement designed to promote prescription, supply, sale or consumption (Directive 2001/83/EC, Articles 86 to 88). EU audiovisual law also bans audiovisual commercial communications for prescription-only medicines and medical treatment, and video-sharing platforms must apply this to advertising on their services, including advertising they do not sell themselves (Directive 2010/13/EU).

In Portugal, advertising a medicine without a valid national authorisation or registration, or one authorised under Articles 92 and 93, is prohibited, prescription-only medicines may be advertised only in technical media for health professionals, and the advertiser, the agency, anyone disseminating the advertising and the owner of the medium are all liable (Estatuto do Medicamento). Health advertising practices fall under Decreto-Lei 238/2015, which bans false claims of guaranteed cure or results or of absence of side effects and is enforced by the Health Regulatory Authority (ERS).

In Brazil, advertising of prescription-only medicines on the internet must be accessible exclusively to professionals authorised to prescribe or dispense them, through an electronic registration system (RDC 96/2008), and ANVISA restated in November 2024 that advertising compounded products to the public is not permitted. CFM Resolution 2.336/2023 forbids physicians to promote medicines not registered with ANVISA, and ANVISA stated on 2 July 2026 that some injectable peptides are not regularised in any category and so are illegal for any health use, including aesthetic use.

In the UAE, advertising or promoting any medical product by any means, social media included, needs approval from the Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE), the federal regulator of medical products since Federal Decree-Law 28/2023, and advertising controlled or semi-controlled products to the public is prohibited (Federal Decree-Law 38 of 2024, Art. 44); an EDE advertising licence requires a valid EDE marketing authorisation for the product, apart from products exempted under Article 5(3) of Federal Decree-Law 38 of 2024. In Dubai, the DHA bans misleading or unproven peptide claims, such as anti-ageing, cell regeneration or improved appearance, unless the use is approved within the product's regulatory status, and requires any promotion of unregistered materials, including through influencers, to stop (29 July 2026). In Abu Dhabi, the DoH bars advertising peptide therapies without prior approval from the DoH and relevant authorities (31 July 2026), and its compounding standard (August 2026) bars advertising emerging, non-monographed substances to patients or professionals.

prompt.en: A patient shows you the certificate for a research-use-only peptide she injects: 99.1% purity by HPLC with a chromatogram, the correct mass by mass spectrometry, and a lot number that matches her vial. What does it establish?

text.en: That the vial is safe to inject.

why.en: Identity and purity say nothing about sterility, endotoxin or storage, and research-use-only products are labelled not for use in humans.

text.en: That the supplier reports the right molecule at high purity for that lot, and nothing about sterility, storage since testing or a lawful route.

why.en: Correct. A certificate describes a lot; it cannot make the product sterile, pharmaceutical or lawful.

text.en: Nothing at all, because certificates are always forged.

why.en: Some are unreliable, but a lot-specific certificate with spectra is real information. The problem is what it cannot cover.

body.en: Off-label prescribing means using an approved drug for a use its labelling does not cover, and FDA accepts it as clinical judgment. A never-approved peptide has no label to depart from, so prescribing it is use of an unapproved drug. Introducing an unapproved new drug into interstate commerce is a prohibited act under the FD&C Act, and FDA's 2020 warning letter to a compounding pharmacy named BPC-157 and GHK-Cu on exactly this basis.

points.en: Off-label applies only to approved drugs
A never-approved peptide has no label
Compounded is still unapproved

blocks.sourceNote: FDA, unapproved use of approved drugs · 21 U.S.C. 331 · FDA warning letter, Tailor Made Compounding (2020) · Peptide Pocket Guide

body.en: An approved drug, used outside its labelling. FDA accepts this as the prescriber's judgment when it is medically appropriate.
A peptide that was never approved has no labelling to depart from. The Peptide Pocket Guide names prescribing it for what it is, use of an unapproved drug.
A 503A or 503B product is also unapproved. It is lawful only when the substance and the pharmacy meet the statute's conditions.

audioScript.en: Off-label is the phrase to get right first. FDA uses it for an approved drug prescribed outside its labelling, which prescribers generally may do when they judge it medically appropriate. The idea assumes a label exists. A peptide that was never approved has none, so prescribing it counts as using an unapproved drug, and the Peptide Pocket Guide says exactly that. Compounding leaves that answer unchanged. A compounded product is unapproved by definition, and it is lawful only when the substance and the pharmacy meet the statute's conditions. Under federal law, putting an unapproved new drug into interstate commerce is a prohibited act, and in 2020 FDA warned a compounding pharmacy about its BPC-157 and GHK-Cu products on that basis. So write the real category in the chart, every time.

text.en: In the EU, no medicine may be placed on a member state's market without a national marketing authorisation or an EU-wide (central) authorisation (Directive 2001/83/EC, Article 6(1)). A member state may, under its own legislation, allow an unauthorised medicine for an individual patient on a bona fide unsolicited order from an authorised health professional, under that professional's direct personal responsibility (Article 5(1)).

In Portugal, marketing a medicine requires INFARMED's authorisation unless the law provides otherwise (Estatuto do Medicamento), and INFARMED may authorise exceptional use (AUE) of a medicine without a marketing authorisation, for example when it is clinically justified as indispensable and no authorised alternative exists.

In Brazil, ANVISA stated in April 2025 that physicians keep the right to prescribe medicines off-label when they judge that, for a given patient, benefits outweigh risks, while no medicine may be manufactured, sold or supplied before it is registered (Law 6.360/1976, art. 12). ANVISA stated on 2 July 2026 that products presented as peptides including BPC-157 and GHK-Cu that promise aesthetic effects or improvement in health conditions are not registered with ANVISA, and that BPC-157 is not authorised for use as a food supplement.

In the UAE, Federal Decree-Law 38 of 2024 lets a physician prescribe a medical product for a use not in its leaflet, or one never submitted to the Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE, the federal regulator of medical products since Federal Decree-Law 28/2023) for marketing approval, only when necessary, when no equivalent alternative is available and with the patient's approval (Art. 42(1)). In Dubai, the DHA prohibits any peptide product that is not registered or licensed with the EDE and requires registered peptide products to be used strictly within their approved indications (29 July 2026). In Abu Dhabi, the DoH allows peptide therapies only for clinical indications supported by available scientific evidence, after a documented eligibility assessment and with informed consent that covers the product's regulatory approval status (31 July 2026).

body.en: Route and claim decide the regime, whatever the molecule. Here is how each one treats a skin peptide in the US, as checked in September 2026.

blocks.sourceNote: FDA: cosmetic or drug; dietary supplements; off-label use · FDA 503A categories (14 May 2026) · 21 CFR 312.160 · Hormonaly guides

note.en: No premarket approval. A claim to affect structure or function, such as 'regenerates cells', makes it a drug; 'cosmeceutical' has no legal meaning.
The maker is responsible for safety and labelling before sale; FDA acts after products reach the market.
Off-label use of an approved drug is lawful clinical judgment; document the reasoning.
Only when the substance qualifies and the pharmacy meets the statute. Non-injectable GHK-Cu is in Category 1; BPC-157 and TB-500 have no route.
Human use belongs in a clinical trial. A 'research use only' vial is outside any clinical route.

callout.en: Write the regime in the chart in these words, before anything else.

text.en: The UK sorts products the same way, by claim, form and use, into cosmetics, food and medicines; lesson 7.2 set out its route for unlicensed medicines.

In the EU, a product is a medicine by presentation or by pharmacological, immunological or metabolic function, and where it could also fall under another product law, medicines law applies (Directive 2001/83/EC, Articles 1(2) and 2(2)); anything intended to be ingested, inhaled, injected or implanted is not a cosmetic (Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009, Article 2(2)). Food supplements are foods, and a health claim on a food is prohibited unless it is authorised and on the EU lists of authorised claims (Directive 2002/46/EC; Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006, Article 10(1)).

In Portugal, INFARMED is the competent authority for cosmetics and states that products administered by ingestion, inhalation, injection or implantation into the body are not cosmetics (read 25 September 2026). Food supplements are meant to maintain the body's homeostasis, not to prevent, treat or cure disease, and must be notified to DGAV before sale; DGAV warns that notification does not mean a supplement is authorised or compliant.

In Brazil, cosmetic labelling may not carry therapeutic claims for the product or its ingredients (RDC 907/2024, art. 12), and ANVISA stated on 2 July 2026 that injectable cosmetics do not exist and that, if a product is offered in this form, it is an irregular cosmetic. A food supplement is by definition a product for oral ingestion by healthy people (RDC 243/2018), and it may use only constituents on ANVISA's authorised list (IN 28/2018).

In the UAE, Federal Decree-Law 38 of 2024 makes cosmetics with a medical effect on the skin, hair or nails, and food supplements, medical products regulated by the Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE, the federal regulator of medical products since Federal Decree-Law 28/2023), while ordinary cosmetics need a MoIAT conformity certificate (Cabinet Resolution 18/2014); an EDE classification letter settles whether a product needs EDE marketing authorisation and in which regulatory category. In Abu Dhabi, the DoH keeps topical cosmetic peptides with no systemic effect on existing pathways as low-risk products, while systemic, regenerative or weakly evidenced peptides face enhanced controls (31 July 2026).

body.en: A 52-year-old patient, three weeks after a fractional laser treatment, asks you to prescribe compounded BPC-157 injections 'off-label' to speed healing. She has found a pharmacy willing to make it and shows you its certificate of analysis. This is a fictional case built from the module's sources, and one response is clearly best.

points.en: BPC-157 has no approval, so there is no label to go off
It has no 503A route; FDA staff advised against listing it
A certificate describes a lot and creates no route

notice.en: BPC-157 has no approved use, so 'off-label' does not apply

label.en: Prescribe it as off-label use and file the certificate in her chart.

why.en: Off-label presupposes an approved drug. BPC-157 has no approval and no 503A route, FDA has warned a compounder about it, and a certificate changes neither fact.

label.en: Decline to prescribe it. Explain the evidence and the US status in plain terms, return to the aftercare plan her treating clinician set, and record her request, what you explained and her decision.

why.en: Right. You keep the conversation, give her the real category and the grade, and leave a chart note a reviewer can follow.

label.en: Suggest she buy research-grade BPC-157 with a good certificate and come back for monitoring.

why.en: Research-use-only products are labelled not for use in humans, and the Peptide Pocket Guide treats steering a patient to them as practising medicine, with the liability that follows.

followUp.en: Chart it in these terms: the product, its regulatory status, the evidence you quoted, the alternatives you discussed and her decision.

prescriber.en: You decline, explain, and document the request, the product's status in those words, the evidence you quoted and the alternatives you offered.

clinical-staff.en: If a patient asks you to arrange or give a compounded or research peptide, record the request and the product details and pass it to the prescriber; do not agree to administer it.

advisor.en: You explain that BPC-157 has no approval and no lawful compounding route in the US, and that decisions about her healing belong with her treating clinician.

text.en: In the EU, no centrally authorised medicine containing BPC-157 was found in the Union Register or in EMA's data on authorised, refused and withdrawn medicines (searched 25 September 2026).

In Portugal, no medicine containing BPC-157 is listed in INFARMED's Infomed register, which includes authorised, lapsed and revoked products (searched 25 September 2026). A compounded medicine may use only raw materials listed in the Portuguese or European pharmacopoeia, another European pharmacopoeia or compendial scientific documentation (Decreto-Lei 95/2004).

In Brazil, ANVISA stated on 2 July 2026 that BPC-157 is not authorised for use as a food supplement, and that any substance must have passed efficacy and safety assessment before it can be compounded.

In the UAE, no registered product containing BPC-157 was found in the register of the Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE), the federal regulator of medical products since Federal Decree-Law 28/2023 (searched 25 September 2026). In Dubai, the DHA prohibits any peptide product that is not registered or licensed with the EDE (29 July 2026). In Abu Dhabi, the DoH's compounding standard (August 2026) treats peptides as high-risk substances and lets novel substances of unknown risk be compounded only if monographed, a component of an approved medicine or listed on the DoH Registry for Compounded Substances.

audioScript.en: A fictional patient, built from this module's sources, is fifty-two and three weeks past a fractional laser treatment. She asks you to prescribe compounded BPC-157 injections off-label to speed her healing. A pharmacy is willing to make it, and she shows you its certificate of analysis. Three facts shape your answer. BPC-157 has never been approved, so there is no label to prescribe around. It has no 503A route, its nominations were withdrawn, and FDA's own reviewers advised against listing it in July 2026, noting a lack of evidence that it works even for the condition they studied. And a certificate describes a batch, which leaves sterility and legality exactly where they were. Decide how you will answer her.

body.en: Compounded BPC-157 injections, prescribed 'off-label' after laser resurfacing, with a pharmacy's certificate in hand.
Never approved. No 503A route, nominations withdrawn, and FDA staff advised against listing in July 2026.
One lot's identity and purity, as the supplier reports them. Sterility, storage and legality sit outside it.

text.en: In the EU, a member state may, under its own legislation, allow an unauthorised medicine for an individual patient on a bona fide unsolicited order from an authorised health professional, under that professional's direct personal responsibility (Directive 2001/83/EC, Article 5(1)).

In Portugal, a physician who prescribes a magistral formula must satisfy themselves of its safety and efficacy, including possible interactions (Decreto-Lei 95/2004), and a patient-specific exceptional-use authorisation (AUE) always needs an individual clinical justification that the medicine is indispensable (Deliberação 840/2023, 31 August 2023).

In Brazil, ANVISA stated in September 2025 that using an unregistered imported medicine is entirely the responsibility of the patient and the prescribing physician, and in April 2025 that off-label prescribing of a registered medicine rests on the physician's judgment that, for a given patient, benefits outweigh risks.

In the UAE, Federal Decree-Law 38 of 2024 allows prescribing outside a product's leaflet, or a product never submitted to the Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE, the federal regulator of medical products since Federal Decree-Law 28/2023) for marketing approval, only when necessary, with no equivalent alternative available and with the patient's approval (Art. 42(1)). In Abu Dhabi, the DoH requires a documented eligibility assessment before peptide therapy and documented informed consent covering expected benefits, uncertainties, risks, alternatives and the product's regulatory approval status (31 July 2026). In Dubai, the DHA does not permit injections or intravenous therapies for 'wellness', 'recovery', 'detoxification' or 'energy enhancement' without a documented medical indication and treatment plan (29 July 2026).

title.en: Final check · Hormones and Peptides for Skin

prompt.en: A single-cell RNA atlas predicts that a skin cell type can make a hormone. What would move that finding toward proof of secretion?

text.en: Showing the hormone protein and its release by those cells, then its effect in tissue or in people.

why.en: Correct. RNA is the first rung; protein, release and function are the next.

text.en: Finding the same RNA in a second atlas.

why.en: Replicating the RNA confirms the transcript, which is still a prediction about secretion.

text.en: Finding the hormone's receptor RNA in neighbouring cells.

why.en: That predicts a possible receiver; it does not show the hormone is made or released.

rationale.en: Transcriptomic maps predict capacity; secretion and function need protein-level and functional evidence, and clinical use needs human trials.

prompt.en: Which finding is a local cutaneous feedback loop rather than systemic endocrine signalling?

text.en: Skin-made vitamin D3 carried by the blood to the liver.

why.en: That is the skin supplying a whole-body hormone system: skin to body.

text.en: Human scalp follicles in culture secrete cortisol and then reduce their own CRH.

why.en: Correct. Made, sensed and fed back within the follicle, with no systemic connection.

text.en: Thin skin and striae in Cushing syndrome.

why.en: Circulating cortisol excess acting on the skin: body to skin.

rationale.en: A local loop is made and used within the skin; systemic signals travel through the blood, in either direction.

prompt.en: Why can a blood or saliva cortisol level not tell you how much cortisol a patient's skin is generating?

text.en: Because 11β-HSD1 regenerates cortisol inside skin cells, and local availability is regulated independently of circulating levels.

why.en: Correct: a mechanism shown in human skin samples and mice.

text.en: Because skin cells cannot make or activate cortisol.

why.en: They can: skin expresses an HPA-like axis, and 11β-HSD1 regenerates cortisol locally.

text.en: Because saliva and blood cortisol tests are unreliable for everything.

why.en: Late-night salivary cortisol is a first-line test for Cushing's syndrome; it measures systemic cortisol, which is a different question.

rationale.en: Local tissue cortisol and systemic cortisol are separate: the first is a research mechanism, the second is what diagnostic tests measure.

prompt.en: A patient asks whether starting hormone therapy at menopause will stop her wrinkles. Which answer fits the evidence?

text.en: Yes: estrogen rebuilds collagen, so her wrinkles will improve.

why.en: Small trials show thicker skin, but the largest trials found no difference in wrinkles.

text.en: It may thicken the skin a little, the largest trials found no difference in wrinkles, and skin is not a reason to start; hot flashes or vaginal symptoms are worth discussing with a prescriber.

why.en: Correct: a secondary effect, and an indication-led decision.

text.en: It has no effect on skin at all.

why.en: Small RCTs do show gains in thickness and collagen; what is unproven is a visible wrinkle benefit.

rationale.en: Separate structural effects (small trials) from visible ageing (large trials) and from indications (symptoms and bone).

prompt.en: A colleague says tirzepatide is 'GRADE A', so its effect on the face must be well established. What is wrong with that reasoning?

text.en: Nothing: a drug's grade applies to all of its effects.

why.en: Grades attach to a specific outcome in a specific population. The pivotal trials measured weight and never the face.

text.en: Grades attach to outcomes: weight loss is A from large randomized trials, while facial change rests on small observational studies.

why.en: Correct. One grade per outcome.

text.en: Tirzepatide has no GRADE A evidence for anything.

why.en: It does, for weight management and type 2 diabetes, from large randomized trials such as SURMOUNT-1.

rationale.en: An evidence grade belongs to a statement, not to a molecule. SURMOUNT-1 supports an A for weight loss; facial change rests on a 20-patient imaging study and a patient survey (C to D), and no randomized trial has measured the face.

prompt.en: Which statement about the gut–skin link is best supported by the evidence?

text.en: Probiotic capsules reliably clear eczema by repairing the gut barrier.

why.en: Pooled trials show little or no difference in patient-rated eczema symptoms.

text.en: Metabolic endotoxaemia is shown in mice and small human studies, but restoring the gut barrier has not been shown to improve disease outside the gut.

why.en: Correct. Mechanism in mice and short-term human physiology; no proof that barrier repair helps the skin.

text.en: A zonulin blood test identifies patients whose skin disease comes from a leaky gut.

why.en: A widely used zonulin assay detects proteins other than zonulin.

rationale.en: High-fat feeding raises circulating endotoxin in mice and briefly in healthy men; a leading review finds it unproven that restoring barrier function improves disease outside the gut, and Cochrane found little or no patient-rated benefit from probiotics in eczema.

prompt.en: Which statement about topical GHK-Cu keeps its evidence and its regulatory status apart correctly?

text.en: It is GRADE C on small trials, and in the US its non-injectable form sits in 503A Category 1, which means under evaluation.

why.en: Correct. Two separate answers: small-trial human evidence, and an enforcement posture that is not an approval.

text.en: Its Category 1 listing shows FDA has found it effective for skin.

why.en: Category 1 means FDA is still evaluating; it says nothing about efficacy.

text.en: Its copper-enzyme mechanism makes its evidence grade A.

why.en: A plausible mechanism is not human evidence; the trials are small (C).

rationale.en: Mechanism, human evidence and regulatory status are separate registers; GHK-Cu scores differently on each.

prompt.en: Oral collagen trials pooled together look positive. What did splitting them by funding and quality show?

text.en: The benefit held in every subgroup.

why.en: It did not: independent and high-quality trials showed no effect.

text.en: The benefit appeared only in pharmaceutical-funded and lower-quality trials.

why.en: Correct — Myung and Park, 2025, 23 RCTs.

text.en: Independent trials showed harm.

why.en: No harm signal was reported; the finding is about absence of benefit.

rationale.en: Funding and study quality can explain a pooled effect; ask who ran the trial before what it showed.

prompt.en: Which statement about afamelanotide and Melanotan II is accurate?

text.en: Afamelanotide is approved (EU 2014, US 2019) only for erythropoietic protoporphyria; Melanotan II is approved for no indication, and regulators in the US, UK and Australia have warned about it.

why.en: Correct. Same receptor family, different molecules, and only one has an approval, for one rare disease.

text.en: Afamelanotide's US approval covers cosmetic tanning.

why.en: The US indication is to increase pain-free light exposure in adults with EPP; tanning is not an approved use.

text.en: Melanotan II became approvable once FDA reviewed it for compounding.

why.en: Its compounding nomination was withdrawn, and FDA's page lists serious safety risks. A review is never an approval.

rationale.en: Approval attaches to a specific product and indication; a shared receptor transfers neither evidence nor legal standing.

prompt.en: A patient asks about a PTD-DBM hair spray. Which grade fits its evidence, and why?

text.en: A, because it acts on the central Wnt pathway of hair growth.

why.en: A plausible pathway is mechanism, and grades rest on human evidence.

text.en: D: one 2017 study in mice and scalp tissue from the developer's group, and no human trial published or registered as of September 2026.

why.en: Correct. Animal and tissue data only, from one group with a commercial link.

text.en: C, because small human trials show regrowth.

why.en: No human trial of PTD-DBM exists, small or large.

rationale.en: Grade the human evidence, then say who produced it; a strong mechanism with no trial in people is D.

prompt.en: In the US, as of September 2026, which statement about growth-hormone secretagogues and 503A compounding is accurate?

text.en: Ipamorelin and CJC-1295 are on the 503A bulks list, because clinics compound them widely.

why.en: Neither is on the list. FDA's advisory committee voted against ipamorelin in 2024, and both 503A nominations were withdrawn.

text.en: None of them is on the 503A bulks list; ibutamoren is in FDA's Category 2 for a heart-failure signal, and the ipamorelin and CJC-1295 nominations were withdrawn.

why.en: Correct, dated to FDA's category documents of April and May 2026.

text.en: Sermorelin is an FDA-approved product marketed for adult anti-ageing.

why.en: No sermorelin product is marketed in the US. Its former approvals were for children with GH deficiency and for diagnostic testing.

rationale.en: Popularity and compounding volume are not regulatory standing; check the live FDA lists and name the date.

prompt.en: Why does a 'low' IGF-1 in a healthy 60-year-old not, on its own, justify growth-hormone therapy?

text.en: IGF-1 falls normally with age, and trials in healthy older adults show small body-composition gains with more oedema, joint pain and glucose problems.

why.en: Correct. The somatopause is physiology, and the trials point against treatment.

text.en: Because growth hormone has no effect on skin at all.

why.en: GH acts on dermal fibroblasts, and GH excess visibly changes skin. The problem is the balance of benefit and harm in healthy adults.

text.en: Because IGF-1 cannot be measured reliably.

why.en: IGF-1 is a standard test. The point is to read it against an age-matched range and to treat a diagnosis.

rationale.en: Treat confirmed deficiency, not ageing: age-adjusted ranges plus the healthy-ageing trials.

prompt.en: In GRADE, what does a certainty rating attach to?

text.en: A single well-run trial.

why.en: GRADE rates a body of evidence, never one study on its own.

text.en: The molecule, across all its uses.

why.en: The same molecule can be high certainty for one outcome and very low for another.

text.en: A body of evidence for a specific outcome.

why.en: Correct. Certainty belongs to an outcome, across the studies that address it.

rationale.en: Name the outcome before you name the grade; risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision and publication bias can each lower it.

prompt.en: Under section 503A, in what order does the statute let a bulk substance qualify for compounding?

text.en: The bulks list first, then a monograph, then a component of an approved drug.

why.en: Reversed. The bulks list is the last route, open only when the first two are not.

text.en: A USP or NF monograph first, then a component of an approved drug, then the 503A bulks list, with a valid certificate of analysis in every case.

why.en: Correct. The routes are hierarchical, and the certificate and a registered manufacturer are conditions throughout.

text.en: Any substance whose certificate of analysis shows high purity.

why.en: A certificate is a condition, never a route on its own.

rationale.en: The statute's routes are hierarchical, and as of September 2026 no peptide sits on the six-substance bulks list.

answer.en: The Hormone Cell Atlas (Fei, Huang-Doran et al., Science 2026) read RNA for 379 hormone and receptor genes in about 14 million cells and nuclei from 47 human tissues and predicted which cell types could make or respond to hormones. Its own authors call these predictions putative and hypothesis-generating: RNA shows capacity, not secretion or effect. Treat any 'skin has receptors for it' product claim as a hypothesis until protein, function and a human trial back it. A few skin outputs are established in people, such as vitamin D3 formed under UVB and released into the blood.

Senescent cells accumulate in human epidermis and dermis with age, and in one cohort their number tracked with wrinkles and perceived age: an association. Their secretions (the SASP: IL-6, IL-8, matrix-degrading enzymes) were defined in cultured cells. Evidence that clearing senescent cells improves ageing comes from mice; human data are small open-label or exploratory pilots measuring tissue markers. The one randomized study in skin (topical rapamycin, a senomorphic, 2019) was small and exploratory: it lowered p16, and clinical change was only described. No adequately sized trial with clinical skin-ageing outcomes was found (September 2026). In mice, clearing senescent cells during healing slowed wound closure. The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide advises confining senolytics to clinical trials. This course gives no doses or product advice; daily sunscreen and topical retinoids are the levers with human trials, and a prescriber decides on any treatment.

Most 'cortisol face' is puffiness from sleep, alcohol, salt and weight, as the Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide describes it. Endogenous Cushing's syndrome is rare (two to three new cases per million people a year), and its commonest form comes from a glucocorticoid the patient is using, so ask about tablets, inhalers, injections and creams, including skin-lighteners. The features that best discriminate Cushing's are easy bruising, facial plethora, proximal muscle weakness and reddish-purple striae wider than 1 cm; a round face alone is a weak signal. If several are present and progressing, the next step is formal testing arranged by a prescriber and an endocrinologist, not a supplement or a consumer cortisol panel. Local skin cortisol (11β-HSD1) is a research mechanism with no approved treatment.

Estrogen acts on receptors in skin. In small trials, hormone therapy thickened skin and raised collagen (graded C here). The largest trial on facial skin (485 women, 48 weeks) and a four-year trial in recently menopausal women found no difference in wrinkles. In the US, as of February 2026, approved uses of menopausal hormone therapy are hot flashes, vaginal and vulvar symptoms and, for some products, preventing bone loss; skin is not an indication and is never the reason to start. Compounded 'bioidentical' hormones lack efficacy and safety data, and an over-the-counter 'hormone cream' is an unapproved drug under US rules. In the UK, HRT products are prescription-only medicines licensed for oestrogen-deficiency symptoms and, for some, for preventing osteoporosis; skin is not among their uses, and a compounded 'bioidentical' hormone is an unlicensed medicine that MHRA guidance places behind any licensed product that meets the need. For skin, daily sunscreen and a prescription retinoid have better evidence. This course gives no doses; hormone therapy decisions belong with a prescriber.

keys: should i stop ozempic because of my face

answer.en: 'Ozempic face' describes facial hollowing and laxity during weight loss on incretin drugs. Mechanism: losing fat deflates the superficial facial fat compartments and unmasks laxity already present. Human evidence is observational and small: one retrospective imaging study of 20 patients found a median 9% loss of midface volume, mostly superficial, about 7% per 10 kg lost (D), and a survey of 1,226 patients found sagging, facial volume loss and hair shedding reported more often the more weight was lost (C). No randomized trial has measured the face. Regulatory status (US, September 2026): semaglutide (Ozempic, Wegovy) and tirzepatide (Mounjaro, Zepbound) are FDA-approved for type 2 diabetes, chronic weight management and further heart, liver and sleep-apnoea indications. Their labels list hair loss (about 3–6% on drug against about 1% on placebo, mostly in women, linked to weight reduction) but not facial volume loss. In the UK (September 2026), Ozempic is licensed for type 2 diabetes, Wegovy for weight management and cardiovascular risk reduction, and Mounjaro for both type 2 diabetes and weight management; UK product information also lists hair loss, and MHRA says retatrutide is not authorised in the UK. Open question: whether the drugs act directly on facial fat, beyond weight loss, rests on cell studies. In practice: raise facial and hair changes before treatment, record concerns with consented photographs, refer restoration requests to a qualified aesthetic clinician, and take any question about stopping or changing the medicine to the prescriber. The course gives no dosing advice.

Mechanism: bacterial lipopolysaccharide crossing a leaky gut barrier ('metabolic endotoxaemia') drives inflammation and insulin resistance in mice, and a single high-fat meal briefly raised plasma endotoxin in a study of 12 healthy men (D). Human evidence for skin: an independent Cochrane review of 39 trials found probiotics probably make little or no difference to patient-rated eczema symptoms (B); a 2024 meta-analysis in children without food allergy reported small score improvements (C); one small randomized trial found rosacea improved after small-intestinal bacterial overgrowth was treated (C). A leading review concludes it is unproven that restoring barrier function improves disease outside the gut, and a widely used commercial zonulin assay detects proteins other than zonulin. A fibre-rich diet has strong evidence for cardiometabolic outcomes and has not been tested on skin outcomes. The Hormonaly guide grades the 'leaky gut' repair stack (L-glutamine, zinc carnosine, BPC-157) D; in the US, BPC-157 is not on the 503A bulks list as of September 2026. In the UK, an unlicensed medicine can be supplied as a 'special' only for an individual patient's special clinical need that no licensed product meets, on the prescriber's responsibility. Start with diet, metabolic health and the skin diagnosis; investigational peptides come last, if at all, and any injected or research peptide needs a prescriber.

Topical GHK-Cu has a plausible copper-enzyme mechanism and small-trial human support (GRADE C); injected GHK-Cu has no randomized trials and commonly irritates. In the US, as of FDA's 14 May 2026 list, non-injectable GHK-Cu is in 503A Category 1 (under evaluation, not approved); the injectable route is excluded. In the UK, a GHK-Cu serum presented for appearance is regulated as a cosmetic, and cosmetics law excludes anything injected; MHRA decides from its claims, form and use whether an injected product is a medicine, and a medicine with no UK marketing authorisation may not be sold, supplied or advertised. This course gives no doses or sourcing advice — for an individual patient, that is the prescriber's decision.

BPC-157's evidence is rodent studies from one group plus uncontrolled case series; no randomized efficacy trial in people has been published in full (September 2026); the one randomized trial FDA found, in ulcerative colitis, exists only as a 2005 meeting abstract and showed no significant difference from placebo. TB-500 is a seven-residue fragment of thymosin beta-4 that has never been trialled; KPV has only mouse data. GLOW and KLOW are marketing names for untested blends. FDA's advisory committee reviewed BPC-157, KPV and TB-500 in July 2026 — advice only; they are not on the 503A bulks list. In the UK, a medicine with no marketing authorisation may not be sold, supplied or advertised, and MHRA's largest seizure of unlicensed weight-loss medicines, in May 2026, included peptide products. New pigmentation while using research-use-only peptides is a red flag: stop, record the product and source, and get it assessed.

Afamelanotide (Scenesse) is an MC1R agonist approved only for erythropoietic protoporphyria (EU 2014, US 2019; licensed in the UK, where NICE did not recommend it for NHS use in 2023), on the strength of two sponsor-funded phase 3 trials; even there, the US label recommends a full-body skin examination twice a year. Melanotan II is a different, non-selective molecule approved for no indication. Its only controlled human data are two tiny 1990s studies, and case reports describe darkening and new moles, nail pigmentation, melanomas in people with other risk factors (causation unproven), priapism and rhabdomyolysis. FDA (April 2026), MHRA (April 2024) and TGA (August 2026) have all put warnings on record. If someone has used it: stop, record the product and seller, examine the skin and nails, and refer changing moles; a personal or family history of melanoma makes it an absolute no in the endocrinology guide. This course gives no doses or sourcing advice.

PTD-DBM releases a brake (CXXC5) on Wnt signalling; its whole evidence is one 2017 mouse and tissue study from the developer's group, with no human trial published or registered as of September 2026 (grade D). Zinc thymulin is a zinc-dependent thymic peptide with no indexed human hair study (grade D). In the US, on FDA's 14 May 2026 lists, thymulin acetate is in 503A Category 3 and PTD-DBM is on no list; neither is on the bulks list. Hair loss starts with a workup (pattern, trigger, patches, androgens; ferritin and TSH in everyone), and the approved options, minoxidil, finasteride in men and baricitinib for severe alopecia areata, carry grade A evidence. In the UK, a men's minoxidil foam is on general sale, finasteride for hair loss is a private prescription carrying MHRA's strengthened warnings on depression and sexual dysfunction (May 2026), baricitinib is licensed for severe alopecia areata, and a peptide spray made up for one patient would be an unlicensed special that MHRA guidance places behind any licensed product that could meet the need. This course gives no doses or sourcing advice; treatment choices belong with the prescriber.

Tesamorelin is the one peptide on this axis with approval-grade evidence: two phase 3 trials and US approval (2010) for excess abdominal fat in adults with HIV-associated lipodystrophy, GRADE A for that use only. Sermorelin, CJC-1295 with DAC and ipamorelin have human hormone-level data but no trial showing a clinical or skin benefit; CJC-1295 without DAC and IGF-1 LR3 have no published human studies (this course grades all of these D). In the US, as of FDA's lists of April and May 2026, no growth-hormone secretagogue is on the 503A bulks list; ibutamoren (MK-677) is in Category 2, and the CJC-1295 and ipamorelin 503A nominations were withdrawn. Growth hormone itself is approved for diagnosed deficiency and a few growth disorders, and knowingly distributing it for anti-ageing is a federal offence in the US. In the UK, somatropin is a prescription-only medicine and a Class C controlled drug, and MHRA's products database holds no product information for tesamorelin, sermorelin or ipamorelin (September 2026). This course gives no doses or sourcing advice; for an individual patient, that is a prescriber's decision.

keys: do growth hormone peptides cause cancer

answer.en: Signs of growth-hormone excess include puffy, thickened skin of the face, hands and feet, oily skin, more sweating, skin tags, acanthosis nigricans, tight rings or shoes, night-time tingling and carpal tunnel symptoms. On GH-axis drugs, fluid retention with swelling and joint pain is common and usually settles when treatment stops. The Endocrine Society recommends IGF-1 testing when typical acral and facial features are present, so route these patients to a prescriber or to endocrinology. On cancer, keep four answers apart: the IGF-1 receptor drives cell growth (mechanism); higher natural IGF-1 goes with modestly higher risk of some cancers (observation); GH replacement in true deficiency has not shown a clear risk in large cohorts; and for secretagogues or IGF-1 LR3 used for skin, long-term cancer data do not exist (open question).

GRADE rates certainty for a specific outcome across a body of evidence: high, moderate, low or very low (the Hormonaly guides print A to D). Randomized trials start high; certainty drops for risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision or suspected publication bias. Industry-sponsored studies more often report favourable results (Cochrane, 2017), so ask who ran and paid for the trials. A grade is separate from legal status: check both, and never let a mechanism raise a grade. This course gives no doses or sourcing advice.

In the US, a 503A pharmacy may compound only from a substance that meets a USP or NF monograph, or else is a component of an approved drug, or else is on the 503A bulks list (six substances, none a peptide, as of September 2026), and it needs a valid certificate of analysis. A certificate is the supplier's report on one lot: mass spectrometry for identity, HPLC for purity, plus endotoxin and microbial results. It cannot prove your vial is that lot, how it was stored, or that it is sterile or lawful. 'Research use only' products are labelled not for use in humans, and 'off-label' applies only to approved drugs. In the UK, an unlicensed medicine reaches a patient as a 'special', made by a licensed specials manufacturer to a prescriber's order for one patient's special clinical need, or as a medicine a pharmacist prepares against a prescription; MHRA guidance ranks a UK-licensed medicine, even used off-label, ahead of an unlicensed one, and specials may not be advertised. This course gives no doses or sourcing advice; for an individual patient, that is the prescriber's decision.

assessmentPlan.plan: Case-based multiple-choice assessment evaluating learner ability to distinguish local cutaneous neuroendocrine feedback loops from systemic endocrine signaling.
Clinical scenario evaluation requiring learners to analyze patient photographs and history to triage systemic endocrine disorders from aesthetic dermatologic complaints.
Evidence appraisal activity where clinicians formulate a patient counseling and monitoring strategy for facial structural changes during incretin-mediated weight loss.
Structured evidence-grading exercise requiring learners to assign GRADE ratings to published clinical endpoints for topical cosmetic and repair peptides.
Patient safety triage vignette evaluating a patient disclosing unapproved melanocortin peptide use, focusing on dermatoscopy monitoring and systemic toxicity risks.
Diagnostic chart-audit exercise analyzing laboratory markers (IGF-1, glucose) and physical signs to detect adverse effects and contraindications for GH-axis modulators.

Quality verification assessment requiring learners to audit a simulated peptide Certificate of Analysis (COA) and marketing dossier for regulatory compliance, purity standards, and adulteration hazards.
Pillar-tagged questions across all seven modules; rationale on every option; no question answerable from marketing language alone.

components: One adversarial co-design conversation: the learner builds an evidence-graded answer to a fictional patient's request for a named skin peptide, while the agent presses on evidence, regulatory status and safety.
Dossier output: appraisal of a simulated Certificate of Analysis and marketing sheet (module 07 pattern), with the patient conversation the learner would have.
Evaluation: agent pre-grade, then faculty gate (reviewer of record).
